BasePK: 3775364

Speech:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to be the final speaker on this very important two days of debate in this House. I do so as the Member of Parliament for some of those people who were on a hunger strike, for some of those who are currently on a hunger strike, and for approximately 800 students at Lakehead University and Confederation College in Thunder Bay, 800 individuals who have chosen to pursue a new future for themselves and for their communities. They see this policy, this change brought in by the Conservative Government to the E-12 guidelines, as limiting the abilities of their brothers and sisters, both literally and in blood, from getting the same kind of access they are now enjoying.
There is nothing that provides greater pleasure than going to the graduation ceremonies at Lakehead University each spring and seeing, year after year, more and more native students graduating. They are graduating from special native study programs, aiming to return to their reserves to work in concert with their peers, their elders and their children. As well, they are aiming to get into the so-called mainstream by applying for jobs
Supply
outside the reserves to provide services to native and non-native alike. As Bob Rosehart, the President of Lakehead University is quoted as saying in Saturday's Star. "These people provide the very positive role models that the communities themselves have been seeking, to say, yes, we can do it. It is not only possible for us to go to Thunder Bay and get an education at the post-secondary level and to come back with a diploma or a degree, but we can bring back with us the knowledge that will assist our communities, be they reserve-based communities or non-reserve communities, in improving our ability to be self-sustainable as a society". That is why it is important that we maximize this investment by the Canadian taxpayers in the educational system.
Just before I spoke there was an exchange between one of my colleagues and the Parliamentary Secretary, who clearly said there would be up to a one year delay for those people who wish to take post-secondary education under this program, but because of a funding cap they would be unable to do so. Who will be the ones delayed? Will they be the high school graduates who come from far northern or remote communities? Will they be told they will have to wait for another year? We know, and there are those who have more expertise in this than I, that the moment you break the educational pattern, the chances of going back to school are virtually nil, particularly for females.
Will it be the adult students who, after years of welfare perhaps, or employment that is not conducive to their community or because we, as a society, have destroyed their natural resources, be they fish, animal, forests or what have you, all of a sudden finally get it all together and say, yes, I have the motivation to go back to school and learn something I was unable to do as a child? More than likely, some did not even complete high school, if they ever went to high school. Are we now to say they will have to wait one more year because we do not have enough dollars and cents. We do not have that extra $9,000 to take them from their remote community to a Thunder Bay or to a Saskatoon or some other city with a university or community college? After those individuals have developed their own motivation, because they know the resources are there, are we going to say no? And does that really mean that we are saying no forever because they will ask, why bother?

April 24, 1989
Supply
Every time we throw another road block in the paths of native Canadians we are doing them a disservice. We should be bending over backwards to give native Canadians full access to our post-secondary education. Not just for a B.A. With all due respect for those who have their B.A., what can you do with a B.A.? You do not even need a B.A. to run for Parliament. You can actually be a high school dropout and get here as well. But the important thing is that they have to have the ability to go on to get into the professions. Doctors, lawyers, accountants, pharmacists and nurses, the whole gamut are important for these communities to have the skills practised by people who are their own, so that they understand the nuances, understand the needs. That is why this is so important.
A lot has been said about the Minister's desire or willingness to keep talking between now and September, and that if the Minister can be convinced that there is a need to change it, he will change it. But the reality is that those individuals who are planning to go to first-year university or first-year community college next year must plan that now.
Our kids are waiting for decisions from the universities as to whether they are accepted. Native kids are too. They need to know that the dollars and cents are in place so that they can make that commitment, so that when school starts on September 4 or 5, they will be there. They need to know about accommodation. They cannot find accommodation the week before university starts. They need to line that up months ahead. If they are coming from one of those small isolated reserves in northern Canada, in northern parts of the provinces, or in an area that is distant from the educational centre, and they are moving not just themselves but are moving children and spouses, they need the time to properly plan and make arrangements in order to have appropriate accommodations for their needs.
That is why we have said put it on hold for now, put a moratorium in place, at least on the negative aspects of the changes, so that the First Nations for the students can work with the Minister and the Department to develop appropriate guidelines that will allow an implementation in September of 1990 so that we do not disenfranchise or delay anybody and that those natives who wish to go to secondary education can do so.

You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

BasePK: 3775396

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour today to present a petition on behalf of a number of Canadians in which they argue that the Government of Canada has failed to take measures to remove Canadian petroleum assets from foreign control. They further point out that the Government of Canada has weakened its ability to ensure that Canadian gas and oil is developed in the national interest. On the basis of these two factors, they petition Parliament to ensure that 100 per cent of the ownership of Petro-Canada remains in the hands of the Government of Canada.

BasePK: 3775405

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate, a debate on a Bill to create a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology. Throughout the next few minutes I would like to bring forward a western point of view.
I want to to point out strongly that I do not want to sound parochial in this matter. After all, westerners, and particularly the good people in my province, feel that they are Canadians first, that they have a lot of faith in this country. We do have in our part of the country some very special concerns. I believe that these concerns must be addressed, and they ought to be addressed in this particular debate. I will touch on some of these concerns as we go along.
We recognize the crucial need to strengthen the economy, particularly in the regions. One way to increase the strength of the economy is to increase our commitment to research and development. In my opinion, that should be at the very top of our list. In an age of technology, research and development ought to be a top priority. One way of doing that is by providing adequate funding, not just bureaucratic shuffling. That is what we see in this particular Bill, bureaucratic shuffling, no real commitment to R and D. I believe this is consistent with this Government's record. I want to point out that since 1984 there has been an appalling neglect of R and D funding.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made some pretty big promises in this regard. For example, he promised a doubling of research and development spending in the first four years of the first mandate of the Government. The Prime Minister did not keep that promise. I want to point out one particular fact. As a percentage of Gross Domestic Product, R and D spending slipped from 1.37 per cent to 1.35 per cent. So much for promises. So much for commitment to managing change in this country.
This is something I want to point out because it was stressed very heavily by the Conservative Party in the last election campaign. We all remember what the Prime Minister said. He said that it was his Party that was best equipped to manage change. How do we manage change in Canada? One way we do that is by staying on the leading edge of technology. It is central to economic growth. It is central to productivity. What have we received from the Government in this regard? We certainly have received promises, shrinking commitment to R and D. We have received bureaucratic games, shuffling people around, creating new positions, renaming Departments. That is not very impressive.
From a western perspective, there are a number of concerns that we have. The western economy, as most people understand, is based on resources and agriculture. That kind of an economy is at the mercy of external forces. We can do almost nothing about these external forces. There are many factors that come into this picture. For example, commodity prices can go up and down in just a matter of minutes. There is the ever present threat of a drought. We had one in the West last year, and it could happen again this year. Oil prices can go up and down at just about a moment's notice. We in the West are always in a rather precarious situation. We need to diversify. We have to give our economy more legs on which to stand. That is why industrial, scientific and technological development is most crucial to the West.
April 25, 1989

Adding to our concerns is the fact that our existing industries, ones that are there already, have been hit by a spate of recent mergers. I would like to mention a couple of them. One is the Molson merger. The other is the purchase of Wardair by PWA. These consolidations have led to fewer jobs. To make matters even worse for our region, high tech firms in the West have closed. Some of them have moved to eastern Canada. I believe that the Government has to take some responsibility in this regard. We have to point out the Government's lack of commitment in the encouragement of secondary industry in the West. That has to be told to the Canadian public.
The Government is weak in this area of encouraging secondary industry in the West. Instead of encouraging development of secondary industry in our region, the policies of the Government appear to have the opposite effect. They appear to have the effect of centralizing industry in central Canada. Instead of recognizing the importance of regional development, instead of developing policies to spur regional development, what do we get? We get bureaucratic shuffling and the renaming of Departments. That is not good enough.
The Government wants to create a Department which would be the focus of developing industrial policies. Fair enough. This particular Bill does not mention the West or what the role of the Department of Western Diversification will be. It does not specify what the role will be of that particular Department. That raises concerns in our minds. We must ask what will be the benefit of this new Department of Industry, Science and Technology to the West. What will be the benefit to our region? We fear that the concerns of the West will be overlooked. We fear this because the mandate for economic development in the West falls outside of the scope of this new Department, outside of its particular mandate. We fear that the economic development of the West will somehow become peripheral and secondary to that of central Canada. It is significant that only the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec are mentioned in this legislation. Our information is that the focus of industrial development will be fixed in central Canada and that the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology will institutionalize that focus.
Industry, Science and Technology
How then will the West fit in? That is the question. Can the Department of Western Economic Diversification deliver? Can it really get for the West the West's fair share? Will the Minister of that particular Department have the stature and the clout to ensure that the West [...truncated]

BasePK: 3775409

Speech:
Thank you. I apologize for that error. I forgot. From now on I will refer to the Minister of Energy.
I just want to say in conclusion that in my opinion the Government has not delivered and has not come through. We have seen the Government abandon the ERDAs. We have seen a lack of commitment to research and development. We have seen a failure to provide Manitoba with its fair share of federal contracts.
In this particular Bill we see the Government's affinity for bureaucratic shuffling and renaming of Departments. We have truly seen the Government's approach to regional development. It is not good enough. We in the West have reason to have doubt. We have reason to be skeptical. We deserve something better. The regions deserve something better. The people of Canada deserve something better.

BasePK: 3775419

Speech:
Ask the Americans. There is defence procurement. There is space agency procurement.
Yet the Government says that when there is a contract to be let, anyone can bid on it. Americans and Canadians will bid on the same basis. The elephant and the mouse are on the same basis for procurement contracts in this country, for contracts that ought to be generating technology in Canada. The Government has taken away ownership, it has taken away procurement, it is taking away the granting and subsidy mechanisms. What kind of research and subsidy mechanisms and what kind of research and development policy will there be? Basic research has been deprived of funding. There has been no decision on how research in industry will be encouraged.
If this new Department is to do any good, it had better start coming to grips with the situation that finds Canada's relative position constantly deteriorating. This is true in government laboratories where morale has been virtually destroyed by the stupidity of the Government's policies and the lack of a long-term plan and it is true of the universities which are being robbed of test tubes, for God's sake, because of the niggardliness of the Government. Every time industry develops something, we sell it off.
We think that the symbolism in the Bill is good. It is probably a good thing that a message will be sent out to the general population that if we are to have economic growth, R and D had better be carried out in Canada. However, the Government will run into trouble because calling attention to that significant, fundamental relationship between research and development, knowledge, economic growth and jobs ought to put pressure on the Government to stop the BS and do something with respect to science, research and development in Canada. Canada's future is at stake.

BasePK: 3775479

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, Air Canada's plan to discontinue jet air service into Stephenville is an absolutely devastating body blow to the economy of southwestern Newfoundland.
Of course the move is a direct consequence of the Government's airline deregulation policy, a policy which decrees that the public's right to an adequate transportation network must play second fiddle to the whims and balance sheets of corporations.
It is a policy which is rapidly translating into inferior air service for people in less populated areas; a policy which, together with rural postal closings and railway abandonments,' is working wonders in the Government's grand scheme to shut down rural Canada.
There is just one way that Air Canada and its service to Stephenville can be saved, that is through the direct intervention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. B. Bouchard). His colleague, the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), already asked him to instruct the National Transportation Agency to hold public hearings on the matter. I now ask the Minister to do exactly that, with a view to according Newfoundland special designation as the NTA Act provides.

BasePK: 3775487

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the revelation that poison gas of some kind was used, fatally, against demonstrators in Georgia is very sorry news indeed. It must be widely condemned as totally reprehensible and never repeated again. Those who made the decision to use it should be brought to justice.
Unfortunately, it seems that the world is on a slippery slope to increased use and increased tolerance of chemical warfare, as we learned to our horror when Iraq employed chemical warfare on his Kurdish population in surely one of the most despicable acts in recent history.
There has been much talk of the need for a treaty to ban all such chemical weapons, as well there should be. It is certainly needed, not just to prevent nations from using such chemicals against each other but also to protect their own citizens. We urge the Government to actively promote such a treaty.

Bill C-ll, as has been noted by other Hon. Members, provides the Government with the authority to borrow $25.5 billion to meet its requirements for the next fiscal year. That is an absolutely frightening number. Most Canadians and probably people in the Chamber can hardly comprehend that in any significant way because it is a number which is beyond anything that most of us would deal with on a day to day basis.
However, we have to consider when we are looking at the borrowing requirements of the Government in what kind of situation the finances of the country are and the budget squeeze that has brought this requirement about, to realize just why we require these funds.
What are the alternatives? Very few or none have been provided by the opposition Parties, even though they have criticized this measure. People must understand what we are doing to work ourselves out of this problem, so that within the next three to four years we can come here following a federal Budget and not be required to present a Bill like this one and continue borrowing.
On this side of the House we are not prepared to dismiss the fiscal position of the Government and to ignore the problem as if it did not exist. If we take a look at government expenditures, and I would like to consider two or three of the larger expenditure areas of government, we can clearly see why it is that we are driven to this additional borrowing as well as putting in place the tax measures that we have.
Senior citizens' pensions represent the largest single expenditure of the Government, in the neighbourhood of $15 billion a year.
Those pensions are indexed so that every year the amount we spend on them will increase by the amount of inflation, running currently at about 4 per cent, so we have an approximate 4 per cent increase simply as a result of that.
Second, the population is growing older. There are more and more people turning 65 and entitled to those pensions.
The result of inflation and people turning 65 will require the Government to find an additional $1.5 billion
Borrowing Authority
this year, just to maintain the existing program, not to improve it, enhance it or increase it.
Let us take a look at a similar situation, the transfer payments to provincial Governments. This is money the provinces use for such things as health care and education. Those amounts are indexed or driven by a formula that provides the provincial Governments an amount each year increased by more than the rate of inflation.
A third element is the interest that the federal Government will pay on the debt. I will speak more on this later. That interest will increase this year by an estimated $6.5 billion. Just to stay where we are and maintain the fiscal position of Government, we need to find an additional $9 billion because of the changes to those items. This means no change in government policy, no growth, nor any increases. This is just to stay where we are to continue with seniors pensions, support for health care and education that most Canadians believe are fundamental requirements of any Government.
Where do we find that $9 billion and any additional amounts that might be required for any other demands placed upon the Government? We have three alternatives. We can cut or reduce other programs, we can increase taxes, and we can borrow additional money to finance the expenditures of government.

One of the other myths that we often hear propagated by the socialist Party, the NDP, is the suggestion that somehow there are deferred taxes around that corporations have not paid and that we should collect those, and if we did we would have no deficit. Even if we were to take that as true and snap all that revenue immediately from those corporations, it is still an amount that is less than $30 billion, which would not eliminate the deficit and certainly would not have anything to do with the debt in this country, which is over $320 billion. Even if we accepted what is totally incorrect and is untrue but is a myth that is being suggested by that party, there would in reality be very little impact on the situation we find ourselves in today.

The fact of the matter, as was pointed out earlier by the chairman of the Finance Committee, the Flon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), is the borrowing requirements for this year have been reduced down to approximately $20 billion per year this year. That is considerably less than the deficit, and there are reasons for that.

By 1990-91, by two years from now, following along with the various measures that have been provided in the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) last week, we will have managed to contain the growth of the national debt to less than the growth in the Gross National Product. That is a very important step and a very important point to reach. If a Canadian has a debt of $10,000 and a salary of $20,000 on which to service and pay that debt, he will find himself in a very difficult situation. That is the situation of the Government of Canada today. But if they are able to get to a position whereby their income is increasing at a more rapid rate than the debt they owe, they will find themselves with room to pay the debt, to reduce it, and eventually work themselves out of the situation. Within two years under the measures that have been provided by the Minister of Finance in this Budget, we will be in that position.
By 1993-94 we will be in the position, all other things being equal, that the Government of Canada will no longer have to borrow money to finance its expenditures. theless, I will say this: however one interprets Parliament's role in deleting article 59, one fact remains-Quebec will have to take a stand.

This commitment of all governments led to the Meech Lake Accord in June 1987.

Member suggests-and with Quebec, to boot- would amount to asking the federal Government to betray its commitment to deal with Quebec's demands first and to postpone other matters until later. Finally, if the Hon. Member is really serious about strengthening minority language education rights he will agree there is a better way to do it. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the Mulroney Government's crushing decision to close or cut back 14 military bases across Canada to save $585 million has caused enormous distress in Canada's regional economies, some of which are dependent on the activities which will now be transferred to other bases. In my Toronto riding, Canada's largest military base may well increase as a result.
It seems that no thought was given by the Government to alternatives which would have spared the regions this devastating cut. I propose to the Government that instead of its present plan, it close the base at Downs-view. Under the Province of Ontario guidelines there would be 25 per cent affordable housing. The urbanization of the base would create thousands of homes, parks and amenities and an economic boom for Toronto, rather than the disaster the Government's present plan delivers to places like Summerside.
To take that example, the closure of CFB Summerside represents a 4.5 per cent total job loss for the Province of Prince Edward Island and the devastation of the economy of that part of the Island.

This military base and air force base goes back to the days of the Commonwealth air training program of 1941-42.
I wish to say at the outset that I do not think that the mandarins here in Ottawa who advised the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight) that that base should be closed down because it was no longer cost efficient realized the human factors. They did not realize the tremendous negative economic impact that that closure
will have on the citizens of Prince Edward Island. It will not only affect Summerside, a town of some 8,000 people, but indeed it will affect the entire Province of Prince Edward Island. It will mean that the second largest employer in the entire province will go out of business. It will mean that 2.2 per cent of the province's total payroll will disappear. It will mean that jobs with wages averaging some $34,000 or $35,000 a year will disappear from the base and the average provincial job with a wage of $17,000 a year will supposedly take its place. Transportation Safety
The federal Government is responsible for the regulation of safety on much of the railway system in Canada. This responsibility has been successfully carried out by a highly qualified, professional staff ever since widespread development of railways was undertaken in this country.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Member for Regina- Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin). There is no question that the amendment put forward by my colleague is an important amendment. In fact, I would submit it is fundamental to the Bill. Members of the House should be aware that what this accident investigation and safety board will do is replace all other accident investigation boards currently at work for the Government of Canada and on behalf of the people of Canada.
For the moment, we have accident investigators operating independently in the air mode, in the marine mode and in the railroad. Of course, the pipeline mode is handled by the National Energy Board. What we are proposing is to consolidate all of those accident investigators in one body and one authority. Whereas for the moment we have perhaps two or three dozen boards made up of two or three dozen board members, what this new Bill will do is just give us five board members for all modes. Hence, the title multi-modal agency. In that instance it becomes not only important but critical that the board members who are appointed not only enjoy the confidence of the Government in the normal way but also have a level of expertise in at least one of the modes covered by a multimodal agency.
We will be proposing a little later this afternoon an amendment to Clause 12. In that amendment dealing with quorums we are asking that a quorum shall be not only three to five members but that at least one of the three must have some expertise in the area of transportation occurrence that is being discussed. It goes without saying that unless there is a guarantee of expertise to begin with-hence the motion of the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin)-it is pretty difficult for the latter amendment that we have put to have any meaning.
June 12, 1989

On this side of the House we certainly embrace the notion that the Government, that is, the Cabinet, ought to be directed in this legislation to ensure by legislative requirement that the people who are given these jobs for a period of seven years be not just people who enjoy the confidence of Cabinet but who, after consultation with the transportation industry, are appointed on the basis of recognized and demonstrated expertise. The period of seven years came about as a result of an amendment made in committee.
One would hope-in fact, one would expect-that whether or not this amendment is in the Bill, this Government or any other Government would make appointments of individuals who have that kind of expertise. However, if it is the expectation of all Members that board members will have expertise and will not merely be friends of the Government of the day of whatever stripe, then let us put it in the Bill. Let us ensure that the people who answer ultimately to Parliament and on behalf of all Canadians for the operation of the multimodal accident investigation board are people who are there as a consequence of their expertise and for no other reason.
I submit that given the history of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, given the general level of lack of confidence by the public in that board because of the controversy and split in the board over Gander, it is more important now than ever before that we not only assure Canadians of a qualified board but that we demonstrate it by insisting upon those qualifications in the Bill.
For that reason I support the amendment which stands in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden.

Madam Speaker, I would like to touch on a few of the things that have been raised by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) today. There is a very fundamental issue that has to be addressed in this debate. It is that one cannot compete if one does not have the fish.
What we are talking about here is the ideological and the philosophical approach that we just heard once again from the Hon. Member from Halifax. He said: "Go talk to the fishermen". He thinks that is the solution.
Let me run through a few of the designs that we see coming out of the ideology of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, or as Alan Fotheringham refers to it, the regressive convertibles.
What is going on in the high seas? We know that Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Korea are involved in a massive drift-net fishery-50,000 miles of drift-nets this year. They are taking between one-fifth and one-third of
British Columbian salmon. What does the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans do? He wrings his hands. He will send five observers out to go on 1,500 boats. He is a real tough guy. He is really out there standing up for Canada. He is a great Canadian.
What does the same Minister of Fisheries do for Alcan? Alcan wants to take all the water out of a river system in British Columbia. It is dealt with in Section 20(10) of the Fisheries Act, one of the oldest constitutional and parliamentary powers in Canada in relation to flowing water and fish. What does he do? He signs on the dotted line. He gives up all powers and turns over those spawning areas in those river systems to the Aluminum Company of Canada so that they can make power to export where? To the United States.
What did he do on the Queen Charlotte Islands when Frank Bevan Logging caused a big slide? The slide went down into the river system and blocked the salmon four seasons in a row so that they cannot get in. We win every way. We win in provincial court. We win in the Court of Appeal. We win in the Supreme Court of British Columbia. The case is on its way to the Supreme Court of Canada so that we can get the logging companies to pay restitution for cleaning out the stream. In the middle of the election what does the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans do? He drops the charges.
There is a design here on the high seas and in the rivers. What about pollution? Some 17 out of the 23 pulp mills in British Columbia have been in significant noncompliance with their permits for more than a year, accounting for 50 per cent of the marine pollution in Canada. We will have fisheries closed right in Prince Rupert. Fishermen cannot even take crab, prawn or shrimp out of the harbour because they are polluted with dioxin. What does the Minister of Fisheries do? He sits on a 600-page report that demonstrates that almost every pulp mill in Canada is in significant non-compliance with the Fisheries Act of Canada. Does he do anything? He does diddly-squat. There are only two places in this country where wool grows. One is on the back of a sheep and the other is inside the skulls of the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. That is clear to anyone who studies this issue for even a moment.
June 15, 1989

Let us go back to where this all began. Let us go back to the grand design. What did the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans say in Prince Rupert? Let me quote his words. We used to have CBC in Prince Rupert but the Toiy ideology was that regions of the country cannot have news and weather. No, we have to get rid of the CBC. Here is what the Minister of Fisheries had to say in Prince Rupert on CBC. I quote: "If we are talking about liberalizing trade, and we are talking about free trade talks, maybe we should be talking about the free flow of fish between the two countries," referring to Canada and the United States.
When the former U.S. Ambassador to Canada, Thomas Niles, was asked out in British Columbia about what some of the articles of the Free Trade Agreement meant when it came to logging he said that his understanding of the Free Trade Agreement was that it would mean that U.S. loggers would be able to come into British Columbia, fell trees, buck trees, load the trees and take those trees back to the United States. That Bill C-8 be amended by adding immediately after line 14 at page 2 the following new clause:

Labour
There are a myriad of concerns with respect to this legislation, as I have addressed in previous comments to the House and throughout the legislative committee process. Obviously these concerns have been shared by my colleagues and by numerous organizations and individuals throughout the country.
As previously mentioned in this House, my colleagues and I support this Bill in principle. By that I mean that older workers need assistance and they have waited long enough for such a program.
I would briefly like to highlight some of the concerns that have been raised pertaining to the legislation. I believe that, although it is definitely an improvement to have a program for older workers' assistance, this legislation has an unusually high degree of selectivity, arbitrariness and subjectivity.
The criteria for eligibility is very broad and does not take into account older workers who may fall between the cracks so to speak. What about older workers who are not part of a major permanent lay-off as designated by the Minister? We still have no idea what the Government will consider as being a major lay-off. Will the Government judge by the number of employees laid off in a region or by the severity of an individual's situation? These lay-offs are to be assessed on a case by case basis.
Given the loosely worded criteria for deciding who qualifies, it is left totally to the discretion of the Minister of Labour as to what constitutes a major lay-off and thus who will be eligible for assistance. The motion I have proposed today will ensure that if the concerns are raised in this area strongly enough to warrant review that the House will do so.
With respect to the federal-provincial partnership of this program, the Government is saying that it will be 70-30 cost shared. It is important to note that Ontario is the only province that has not agreed to participate. British Columbia has recently entered the program. Why has Ontario not agreed to participate? We haven't been given any reasons for its reluctance. Does this mean that older workers from Ontario will not have the same rights and opportunities as older workers from the other nine provinces?
Another concern is how the program will mesh with the UI proposals. How will the design for programs for older workers under the labour force development strategy mesh with POWA? During the legislative committee hearings a multitude of concerns were raised, some of which I outlined a few moments ago and some of which I will outline now. Mr. Speaker, we have before us today government Bill C-2, an Act to establish the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board. At the outset there was some resistance by some Members of the esteemed Standing Committee on Transport during clause-by-clause consideration of the Board to not incorporate the word "safety" in the title of the Act. However, through the insistence of opposition Members we directed the Government's attention to the mandate of the Board, which is found in Clause 7, that is, that "the object of the Board is to advance transportation safety". The Government eventually saw the wisdom of our suggestion and, despite the committee chairman's observation that the title, in his words, "lacked sex appeal" or something very close to that, the TAIB or Transportation Accident Investigation Board was amended to include the word "safety".
I want to make it clear that I do not disagree with the intention of this Bill. In addition to aviation occurrences, the new Board will consolidate and be responsible for investigating occurrences in the modes of rail, marine, and pipelines transportation.
It must be noted that Bill C-2, when enacted, will replace CASB, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. That was a good idea. CASB did its job, conducting close to 700 investigations a year. It gained a solid reputation in aviation circles around the world. However, a grievous split developed in a most controversial case, Canada's worst air disaster, the crash of an Arrow Air chartered DC-8 at Gander, Newfoundland, in December, 1985, which claimed the lives of 248 U.S. soldiers and eight crew members.
Enter CASB. Four of nine board members, all of them intelligent, capable and knowledgeable, with full credentials, disagreed with the report of the Board which concluded that a thin layer of ice on the planes' wings was responsible for the crash. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) endorsed the report which then prompted the four dissenting members to call for public inquiries, not only into the controversial finding that icing caused Canada's worst air disaster, but into air traffic control problems as well.
In light of this and other problems, including the resignation of the Assistant Deputy Minister in charge of Canadian Aviation Safety, who resigned in the midst of controversy over the crash at Gander and the Air Ontario crash at Dryden, the Minister of Transport, instead of attempting to rectify problems that existed within CASB, chose to create a new board, virtually sweeping under the rug any outstanding questions in relation to Gander, Dryden and other problems the Government failed to deal with immediately in air transportation.

Canadians are no more assured of increased safety now than they were in the past. There is nothing in Bill C-2 to prevent a repeat of the circumstances which led to the end of CASB.
What incredibly convenient timing, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Transport appoints an eminent outside authority, Mr. Justice Willard Estey, to review the Gander accident investigation and appoints Mr. Justice Virgil Moshansky to conduct an inquiry into the Dryden accident. On the subject of power, it was the contention of many witnesses who appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport that too much power will be handed to the chairman of the multi-modal board. Under Bill C-2 the chairman will have the power to hire and fire investigators, all the financial power, power to set the agenda, and the power to decide what Board members will do what work; all this power in the hands of a single individual. Let us not perpetuate the problems that existed under CASB where the powers were vested in one individual rather than in the Board as a whole. The chairman must be responsible to the Board.
In the overall scheme of things, the public lost its confidence in CASB because a group of Board members had to move out from under the umbrella of the Safety Board in order to publish their own minority report because a powerful chairman attempted to silence them. We can learn from this, Mr. Speaker. The very essence of democracy means to consider many points of view. We welcome and in fact look toward the divergence of opinion in order to judge effectively. Dissent is healthy. This House is a good example of that, Mr. Speaker. The multi-modal Board must make room for dissenting points of view and accept the variety of opinion. It all works toward ensuring that transportation, whether by air, rail, marine or pipeline, is as safe as it can be for all Canadians. That is the ultimate goal.

The public can have confidence in the fish inspection system due to its multi-facetted nature involving inspection of vessels, unloading practices, raw product, transportation, plants processing practices, and final product. While the Department is taking, and has taken, action to ensure that the Canadian fish inspection system remains as one of the best in the world, the multi-facetted approach provides assurance that the fish now on the market meets standards in spite of the limitations of any one aspect of the inspection program. Any problems that did exist resulted from a lack of central direction and control. In 1986 the Department undertook a major reorganization that, among other things, centralized authority and accountability for the inspection program. As noted in the report, many initiatives to improve management of the inspection program were being planned or were under development at the time of the audit, but at the time of the audit the improvements had not had an impact at the inspector level. Since the audit, a Fish Products Inspection Manual has been issued to inspectors and results are being felt at the field level.

The following outlines the action taken to date in response to specific comments regarding fish inspection which the Auditor General made in his 1988 Report.
-Sampling. The Auditor General raised concerns regarding the Department's sampling plans. The Department has been evaluating an alternative internationally recognized sampling plan for two years and is now implementing major pilot projects to test the new sampling plan under practical conditions. If the pilot projects prove that the new sampling plan performs as expected, the new plan will be introduced early in 1990.

While the "Fish Products Inspection Manual Standards and Methods" is scheduled to be released this year, six (6) specific product standards and methods chapters have already been forwarded to the field for use and other standards and methods will be released shortly. By the end of 1989/90 more than 80 per cent of all fish products will be covered by newly revised standards and methods.
The "Metal Can Defect Manual" will be published this month. The Facilities Inspection Manual will be released as a first draft by July.
These new manuals and standards will complete the task of reissuing a revised set of instructions to all staff.
-Training. The Auditor General raised concerns over training. The Department has been developing national training packages for some time. Inspectors will be evaluated in 1989/90 to determine their specific training needs. Training will be delivered in 37 training modules. Twenty (20) modules are now complete and training will commence in 1989/90. University level courses in sensory evaluation for inspectors started in 1986/87 and are continuing.
-Inspector Testing. Inspector testing continues with respect to tuna. A series of workshops will be held in June to lay the groundwork for testing inspectors evaluations of other products. Work on chemical indicators of spoilage is continuing and will help in the testing of inspectors. A national inspection laboratory was estab-

lished in 1988 in Ottawa and is now equipped and staffed to assist in work on chemical indicators of spoilage.

For jobs that will be available in new ways because we know that the world is changing. The Member can talk about trying to keep people employed in jobs that no longer exist.
I grew up in a small town. Every small town had a railway station, a bakery, a butcher shop, livery stable and a whole range of businesses that no longer exist today. We will never go back to those days. We will not be able to remain where we are. People have jobs today, jobs that will not exist one year, five years or ten years from now. Those jobs will no longer exist. We cannot try to maintain those jobs in a changing world and the man for the products and services they produce is no longer there. What we have to try to do is to find new jobs for those people and ensure that they are adequately trained to fill them. Five million Canadians a year change jobs. So job change is not the issue. Neither is trying to hold onto jobs that are no longer relevant to today's society. Surely what we want to do is train people for the society of the future.
I want to make a few comments about the capitalization and lump sum payments and how they reflect a commitment to change. Really these are an important statement for individual entrepreneurship. There can really be only three classes where workers go on unemployment insurance. Either they are unemployed for reasons beyond their control, they are temporarily out of the workforce for family reasons, or they have chosen not to work.
In the first scenario, when the person is unemployed for reasons of technology or economics, the proposed changes are improvements. Currently the rationale of the UI program is simply that you will continue to receive benefits until you find another job for which you are qualified, or until you go on another form of social assistance. This is not an exceptionally efficient use of finances, as I said earlier. It is a waste of the workers' time and talents, especially since they may be in a situation where there is really no hope of finding the

Unemployment Insurance Act
kind of jobs that they have been doing in the past. By encouraging the person to get additional education or start a new business venture, we are making an unemployed worker into a better and more productive one.
The second scenario, where employees leave for family reasons, is also being improved with these amendments. Expanded maternity leave and a recognition that adoptive parents as well need time to adjust to the additional person in their lives will make for a more responsive program. With women an increasingly important part of the workforce, these revisions help ensure fairness in the system. The same holds true for older workers who do not want to retire at age 65. By extending benefits, the Government is making the system fairer for those older workers who want to continue in the workforce. That is an important measure because while in the past 20 years we have seen high levels of unemployment, these are in large measure the result of the baby boom after the Second World War with those people coming into the workforce.
In the next 10, 15, 20 years the reverse is going to be true. As these people grow older and begin to reach retirement age, we do not have the numbers coming into the workforce. Therefore, while the problem of the 1970s and the 1980s was one of high unemployment, the problem of the 1990s and the years beyond, in my view, is going to be one of shortage of skilled workers. Therefore, I think it is quite appropriate that whereas in the past we were encouraging people aged 65 or even younger to retire from the workforce, for those who wish to continue we should we give them every opportunity to do so.
I would like to make mention of the people in the third category, those people who choose not to work. There is also a group of amendments and increased penalties for those who abuse the UI system. These are also an integral part of an efficient and fair approach. They make it clear that the UI system is for workers and not for conscientious objectors in the workforce.
I want to talk about fairness in the program. I have a great many constituents who come to see me with various complaints. These amendments move to solve some of the problems, but unfortunately not all of them. For example, I suppose that under the current system,
like the old one, it will still probably take several weeks for the contributor to receive the benefits to which he or she is legitimately entitled. That it can take months to receive a cheque strikes most of my constituents as unfair, especially since they are often receiving benefits for which perhaps they have paid over many months or years in the past. I have also heard from workers who could not collect benefits, and I am pleased to see that that issue is being addressed. I have also heard from people in the taxi industry and in the Armed Forces who currently do not believe the system is fair because they pay premiums and do not receive benefits. At some future time I would like to see that addressed.
On a positive note, the current amendments include a series of provisions to address current changes in the labour force, current factors of regional differences in the country. There is really no reason why we should offer the same level of benefits in an area where they have virtually full employment as we offer to an area in which there is less opportunity to find jobs. We know that in some areas of the country people can find work if they wish to. Again, this introduces an element of fairness.
I could speak longer on this topic, Mr. Speaker. I wish I had the opportunity. Maybe I will get that later tonight, but in the meantime I thank you for the time allotted to me and I will complete my remarks another day.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Minister for being present here today. I am sure that by the various speeches made by the Official Opposition he has probably noticed that there are indeed longer-term goals in our society that we must be able to face. We are not simply addressing Bill C-18, an Act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship, but are indeed speaking to the contemporary cultural reality that is Canada. More important, this debate will bring to the forefront some very fundamental questions related to the cultural policy direction that the country is willing to take to the 1990s and the 21st century.
During a period of our country's history when we are challenged by the definition of our cultural identity, it is very important to begin to review the role that multiculturalism plays in our society, indeed what necessitated the implementation of a Multiculturalism Act, what this Act is in fact responding to and, hence, what the purpose is of a separate Department. As a Canadian elected to the House of Commons, I firmly believe that I have the moral obligation to attempt to define what is Canadian culture, what is our Canadian identity.
In this nation we are often faced with a multitude of terms to define and express what is, in cultural terms, our Canadian society. Terms such as "bilingual", "multicultural", "diversity" and "pluralism" are but a few of the expressions that we have used in an attempt to come to grips with who we are and what we are. As far as I am concerned, I view our Canadian cultural reality in multicultural terms, however, not necessarily in total accordance with the traditional meaning of multiculturalism or its usage.
There is no question in my mind that contempory Canadian culture is indeed multicultural. The very essence of this reality can be seen in the many faces of our Canadians citizens. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to ask a few questions and to make a speech in the House this evening, particularly when the Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mr. McDermid) is present, as is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Dobbie), because during my last speech in the House she kept heckling me and I found that rather challenging. The rates of federal sales tax are increased from 18 per cent to 19 per cent on alcoholic beverages; from 10 per cent to 11 per cent on telecommunication services and telecommunication programming services; from 8 per cent to 9 per cent on construction materials; and from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent on all other taxable goods.
The Government maintains that those tax increases will generate an additional $2 billion in its first full year of operation. The tax increases the Government has proposed, along with the others it has implemented since it was first elected in 1984, represent the largest tax increases any government has imposed on Canadians in our history. Frankly, it is a shocking record of financial neglect, financial mismanagement, and ministerial incompetence on a scale we have not witnessed since the Diefenbaker Government in the 1950s and the early 1960s. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Dobbie) laughs. I recognize that laugh, a nervous laugh of those who realize that defeat is imminent. The Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) is getting into the act.
They may feel comfortable in their majority in the House, but they are worried. They know that Members like the Member for Calgary Northeast (Mr. Kindy) will be deserting the Party on crucial votes in the House.

June 26, 1989
Excise Tax Act
Sooner or later, people will come to their senses on the other side and desert the Government in sufficient numbers that bad Bills like this will be defeated on the floor of the House of Commons and we will go to the people to let them decide whether a Bill imposing these kinds of taxes is what they want.
I want to deal with Bill C-20 in the context of the leaky Budget that Members will recall was introduced in the House on April 26. Secondly, it states, "They are enjoyed by individual Members because the House cannot perform its functions without unimpeded use of the services of its Members".
Are the Members in any way impeded from appearing in the House or in committee? Obviously, they are not. So the definition of privilege has obviously not been met in any way by the presentation that has been made by either of the opposition parties today.
But let us look at the question of contempt. According to Abraham and Hawtrey's definitions, the parliamentary dictionary, we see it states on page 80:
Contempt of either House of Parliament-Any act or omission which either directly obstructs the due proceeding of that House or has a tendency to produce that effect by bringing its authority into contempt, e.g. the publication of reflections on the character or conduct of a member in his capacity as a member.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to participate today in this debate. It is an historic debate which establishes a new federal government department responsible for multiculturalism and citizenship.
These are important steps which flow from a landmark study done in 1960, the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism which is properly known as the Laurendeau-Danton report. It noted at that time in recognition of the diversity of the cultural groups found in Canada that "Canadian society, open and modem, should be able to integrate heterogeneous elements into a harmonious system to achieve unity in diversity".
I think much of the debate and differing points of view here relate to the fact that fundamentally, in adding this rich cultural diversity and recognizing it, we add to the fundamental characteristic which is in our constitution officially, the bilingual and bicultural nature of Canada. We are talking about the right for equal treatment and consideration under the laws of Canada.
I am very pleased because this government took an initiative that was started with Laurendeau-Danton in 1971 to establish a policy marking multiculturalism. This department becomes official through this act and I believe, if given adequate resources, can become a great symbol of the reality of our multicultural heritage and of the grandeur of our diverse ethnic mix, something that the people of Canada are becoming more and more aware of every day. We hope that this department can enrich the unique multicultural tapestry that is the Canadian society, enabling us to forge a new era of goodwill in the relationships among our people, notably respect, understanding and tolerance, which is the hallmark of Canadians with very few aberrant moments in our history.
As a new arm of the national government, this department should work to preserve and enhance the fundamental characteristics of Canada which I stated as being tolerant, open, peaceful and democratic. But let us not fool ourselves. The creation of this department is but

I hope that this new department will be able to provide a leadership role so that its efforts, research and findings will become a guiding framework all across government and through this touch all aspects of Canadian life. The challenge is to direct our whole range of national programs toward integrating new Canadians and those who have been here for generations into all aspects of Canadian life in a coherent and proper manner.

I will first address the 9 per cent Mulroney sales tax. What we have here is a massive shift of responsibility from the federal government to individuals, to small business, to low income people, to our elderly and to other levels of government.

The finance minister assured the Canadian municipalities that local government would not be used as a source of new revenue. The technical paper indicates that municipalities are to be rebated a substantial part of the remitted GST. But even so, there are considerable inequalities which cause a contradiction to the minister's over-all commitment.
According to the FCM report it is the failure of the proposed government formula to recognize the extraordinary administrative burden confronting municipalities under GST. There are several types of tax collection and remittance requirements to which they will be subjected. To name a few, they will be faced with the task of tracking the applications of any good or service acquired in order to determine the appropriate GST treatment, and the government formula will vary from municipality to municipality. Some municipalities will be winners and other municipalities will be losers.
Second, compensation for administrative costs applies to small business. Why not municipalities?
Third, cash flow costs are ignored while waiting for the rebate.
Fourth, the burden of a federal tax on top of a provincial tax will increase costs to municipalities beyond the amount recognized in the formula.
Fifth, the commitment of the Minister of Finance to municipalities was that services such as telephone systems, natural gas, hydro, water-they sell their water- would not be subjected to the tax increase, and yet the technical paper states the contrary. The Minister of Finance, in spite of that commitment to the municipalities, has reneged on all those commitments to those municipalities. Their only source of revenue is from the property tax base and whatever grants they are at the mercy to receive from the province and the federal government.
Government members have no one to blame but themselves when faced with a public that has nothing but doubt and cynicism over the government's true motives. First they said it would be revenue neutral then they said it would be visible. On both counts the government lied,

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity I have been given to speak today on the subject raised by Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Samson).
As you know, the Canadian minerals and metals industry tends to expand outside the country, which is necessary.
Canada is the world's largest producer of zinc and uranium and second largest producer of potash, nickel, asbestos and gypsum.
Since Canada's contribution to the demand for these products is still far from its contribution to their supply, it is not surprising that we export large amounts of our minerals and metals at various stages of production.

Canada's contribution in this field is not confined to mining. In addition to the primary extraction of our mineral ores, Canada makes a major contribution to the further processing of this ore. We have a refining and smelting industry of which we can be proud and which, in certain areas, is world class. I shall have more to say about this later.
The motion before the House today would like to see an expanded role for further processing in Canada and I am in full agreement with that objective. In promoting this objective, however, we should not lose sight of some important realities. Competition is very intense worldwide at all stages of the mineral and metal industries. In the past decade we have seen the mining sector having to make some very painful adjustments, cutting its labour force and introducing new technologies in an effort to remain competitive. These adjustments were not easy, but they were necessary and the industry is the stronger for having made them.

October 10,1989
Private Members' Business

In the same way that Canadian mines can close and lose customers to the benefit of foreign suppliers if they cannot keep their prices low, the refining and smelting sector also faces keen competition.
The Government is confident that under the right conditons, these sectors can prosper and develop. For several years now, we have tried to create ideal conditions for the processing sectors to prosper. These efforts are being pursued on various fronts. The first two ways involve increasing Canada's access to world markets and reforming the tax system. These are familiar to all Canadians. These efforts are not particularly directed at the minerals and metals industry, but provide a basis for the long-term growth of all sectors of this industry by allowing Canadian firms to compete effectively on world markets.

This government does not believe that it would be in the long-term interest of Canada's refining and smelting industry to provide it with artificial stimulus. When the protectionist measures were eventually dismantled, as they would have to be, the industry would have to make much more drastic adjustments than if it had been exposed all along to the discipline of foreign competition.
The motion suggests that Canada should discourage the export of unprocessed minerals. I do not think that this would help smelting and refining in Canada. The most efficient smelting and refining companies worldwide would simply find an alternative supply source. Remember that while Canada's resource base is rich, it is not unique. There are many competitors. If Canada is an unwilling seller, there are other suppliers to take our place. The best long term strategy for Canada's mineral processing industry is the rigorous pursuit of efficiency and the gradual build-up of capacity which would allow it to take advantage of Canada's rich mineral wealth.
I would like to repeat for the record the six principal objectives of mineral policy set out in the mineral and metal policy of the Government of Canada in May 1987. They are: to provide a fair and balanced fiscal and regulatory framework; to foster the development of the mineral and metal sector as a foundation for regional
economic development; to promote improved technological performance and increase international competitiveness in all facets of the industry; to assist workers in communities affected by industrial adjustment; to facilitate enhanced mineral and metal exports and access to new and traditional markets; and to provide timely and accurate economic, technological and scientific information required by the industry and by the federal and provincial governments, labour and the general public.
As these objectives make clear, this government appreciates the strong role which mineral development has played and can continue to play in the economic development of Canada's regions. The Government of Canada will continue to provide a supportive environment for the industry in the ways outlined; encouragement of R and D, tax reform, provision of information, trade initiatives and adjustment assistance. However, insofar as the production and investment decisions of the industries are concerned, this government believes that individual firms are in the best position to evaluate the information on which these decisions should be based. The Canadian mineral and metal industry has a strong record of past achievement and we have every confidence that it will continue.

As the member for Sudbury I probably know as much, if not more, than a lot of the people here about mining and refining as it is carried on in my city and province. Falconbridge, on the other hand, does no refining whatsoever in Canada. In the early 1920s, when Falcon-bridge was wishing to refine some of its minerals itself, it found itself in a position where International Nickel controlled all of the patents everywhere except in Norway. Therefore, they were not able to register their patents for refining, or at least in this country or in the United States. So they bought up a closed refinery in Norway and were able to get a patent there and went on with business, and to this day they refine in Norway. The provincial government now gives Falconbridge special permission to ship to Norway.
In the early 1980s, when there was a severe downturn in the mining economy, had we forced Falconbridge to refine locally I do not think we would have a Falconbridge operation in Sudbury at this time. It is very important that when this rule is enforced there is some consideration given to the times. We know that this past year Falconbridge has had some considerable profits, and we are pleased with that. We also know that Falconbridge will be renegotiating this special permission with the provincial governments over the next few years.
I would like to impress upon our provincial governments the fact that we certainly would like to see the investment of some of these moneys that they have made in a refining plant, preferably in our city. It is important that, if that permission is given to ship out, there be considerable reason in terms of investments in properties to offset that. I really believe that if you build a refinery that costs $500 million and creates 300 jobs it may not be quite as good as creating 500 or 600 jobs at a new location and a new mine. From the studies that I have seen, it is clear that in all the countries that have brought in the goods and services tax, within months of bringing in that tax the rate was increased. The latest example from New Zealand is that it went from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent.
I think in every case not only have they raised the tax that they brought in originally, but they increased their spending to meet the cash cow effect, so what we have is a situation where the governments spend more as they get it in, and look less at what their expenditures are.
It is undoubtedly a fact that if this is brought in, as is often proposed by some of the government's friends in the manufacturing sector, and we broaden the base, bring in foods, do away with exemptions, and if we lower the rate, it is simply a matter of time before the rate is raised up. I think all of the people who have appeared before us in committee have agreed to this.
The inflationary factor that is involved in any level of goods and services tax, particularly the one at 9 per cent, will probably be double what the government has originally told us. The spiral effect of inflation which the government has not taken into consideration due to increased prices and increases in wage demands will have detrimental effects on all of the economy of Canada with a probable increase in the value of the dollar and an increase in the level of interest rates. We will have total chaos and perhaps a major recession as a result of this.

For many years there was an export restriction on unprocessed sockeye and pink salmon and herring from the west coast of Canada, but no such restriction on the other species of salmon, Chinook, the coho and the chum species. Meeting the challenge posed by the debt by reducing spending and increasing revenues is a responsibility that we have to present and future generations of Canadians.

BasePK: 3798852

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the laundering of money from drug trafficking is a serious problem in Canada. Until last January when Bill C-61 was enacted, Canadian law never specifically made money laundering a crime. Bill C-61 encourages Canadian banks to establish their own private guidelines on what constitutes suspicious bank deposits.
I would like to commend the Royal Bank of Canada for going one step further by imposing a de facto reporting requirement for all large transactions. Since January, anyone making a large cash deposit at the Royal must sign a declaration of source of funds. That person must provide personal identification such as a social insurance number, passport or driver's licence. The signed form gives the bank permission to disclose the transaction to the police.
So far this year, the Royal has examined close to 100 suspicious accounts, and has reported 76 to the RCMR On October 12, 1989, U.S. criminal charges were laid against a Royal Bank customer after police were tipped off by the bank about suspicious transactions. The Royal Bank should serve as an example for all Canadian banks to follow in the war against drugs.

Accordingly, in 1873, the Dominion Parliament passed legislation for the establishment of a mounted police force for the Northwest Territories to be known as the Northwest Mounted Police.
Three divisions of 50 men each were mobilized at Fort Garry, Manitoba, where training and organization took place during the winter of 1873. Recruitment proceeded and reached a strength of 1,000 by the year 1885.
Once established in the northwest, demands upon the force increased. Members supervised trading practices, provided some relief and medical services to the Indians and they carried out patrols throughout the area. In addition, the force had an economic and cultural impact on the west as many members, upon leaving the force, made the west their home.
Furthermore, by the start of the Klondike gold rush in 1896, the Northwest Mounted Police was already established in the Yukon. From the start, the force carried out almost all the administrative functions of government. Its members acted as land agents, magistrates, police and mail carriers. After the peak of the rush had subsided civil servants had relieved the force of many of its administrative duties. A few years later, the force was also to play a prominent role in opening up the Canadian Arctic frontier.
In 1905, the first contracts were negotiated for the force to act under the direction of the provincial authorities to enforce the criminal laws and local statutes. The force was active in the campaign of the Canadian government to attract settlers to the prairies. By 1914, over a million settlers had arrived. The police became land agents, agriculture experts, welfare officials and immigration officers. By this time, the mounted police had achieved an international reputation for its part in bringing about the orderly development of western
Canada. It is noteworthy to add that the force sent contingents to fight in both World Wars.
In 1920, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, as it had become in 1904, absorbed the Dominion Police which had been responsible for federal policing in eastern Canada. In keeping with its national role, it was renamed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

In accordance with Sir John A. Macdonald's apparent desire to keep the uniforms of the new police force simple, a jacket made of heavy scarlet serge with a wool lining was issued as the tunic for all ranks; dark blue cavalry pattern overalls, black boots and a pillbox cap or white helmet completed the uniform.

I am not talking about one million new cars, I am not talking about trips that would not have otherwise occurred. But what they did not do was the next logical step. In any environmental assessment the most logical step is to measure the impact on the environment. How many more kilograms or kilotonnes of nitrous oxide or carbon dioxide would be emitted in the atmosphere? They did not do that, Mr. Speaker. They just said that one million more car trips, really will not have much of an impact so let's not bother doing a full environmental assessment. Part of the reason why we of the New Democratic Party put forward this motion today is to make the point that we have to treat our world a lot better than we are now.
Any kind of government policy, in this case on taxation, but also on transportation, should have as its uppermost concern the impact on the environment. Let us hope it is in terms of how we can lessen the impact on the environment, not how we can add more like this decision on VIA Rail has done. In this great country of ours, which is such a vast magnificent land, many people live in a very narrow corridor next to the Canada-U.S. border, with some fingers of development in the northern territories. In northwestern Ontario we have had to build around Lake Superior and the Great Lakes in order to get from east to west. We need an integrated system.
It does not make sense for people to be flying from Toronto to Ottawa or Toronto to Montreal, or Montreal to Ottawa when for substantially less money, fuel and land, and much less pollution, we could be using high speed electrified rapid transit between those main communities. Given the congestion of Pearson International Airport, which is not going to be solved by a new terminal, it will be quicker, downtown to downtown, to travel by rail between these cities. Think of the atmosphere, Mr. Speaker. I know that you travel on the trains from time to time. Consider how much easier it is to do business in that particular corridor with the high-tech we now have. On the train we can use cellular phones and have a desk away from home, so to speak. You arrive in a much less frazzled state. We can do with that kind of thing.
It makes sense in some of the regions of the country to use rail, to link Thunder Bay and Dryden for example, or Cape Breton and Halifax, rather than air for these short distances. There are many options for environmentally friendly forms of transport.
That is on the passenger side. What about the freight side? As a country we have to be able to move both raw materials and finished goods. Right now we do it on the basis that because of the high cost of transportation, those people who are farther away will pay more.
From an economic standpoint, dare I say it, we could change a couple of policies and follow the lead of the private sector. Some of the major department stores have what they call a regional pricing policy. We all get the fliers from Sears or Eatons and see that a fridge in Thunder Bay is priced the same as the one in Toronto. We have done it with beer in Ontario. We do it with milk in other provinces. We are required, by the company policy, to include transportation costs in the over-all price so it becomes part of their cost of doing business. Therefore, it is averaged out so that that fridge can be sold in every community at the same price.
One might ask what that has to do with an environmental tax. It has everything to do with it. We are crowding so many people into the golden horseshoe of southern Ontario, mainly because that is where the markets are, the people buy the finished goods. Therefore it makes sense, given the Canadian economy as it is structured now, to locate the plants there. So that means more people come to the golden horseshoe to work and therefore create more demand, and on and on and on. A transportation policy should reflect the environment and land use planning. We so often forget that land use planning is an important environmental consideration.

We will look at it after that and see where we are. The rates go up and down. is nothing in the law to say that we cannot remove some of those funds from the premiums that are being paid. We quite rightly have done that. We have said that the people who will receive training under the UI system will be those who contribute to the fund.
