Basically, at the federal level the government must start by increasing the minimum federal wage which is now the lowest in the country and has not been increased in three years. It should be indexed to the cost of living, just as pensions were indexed several years ago. Second, the federal government must increase family allowances and the child tax credit and index them to the rate of inflation. This money goes directly to low-and middle-income families to pay for food, housing and clothing. Third, the federal government must increase federal financing for low-cost housing.

Supply
Ten years ago, the government financed construction of 30,000 new low-cost housing units per year. Today, this number has dropped to 20,000.

We must also move to bring in child care legislation which has as its purpose and fundamental goal an increase in the number of spaces that will be available for children throughout Canada.
This in itself will help thousands of Canadian women who love their children, who want to care for them but who are now locked into welfare. They cannot afford adequate child care and so are forced to stay home when they would prefer to be spending part of their time working in the economy out of the house and part of their time looking after children but they know that they cannot leave them if there are not adequate child care spaces available.
One recent survey showed that there were over 21,000 Canadian women who specifically said they would prefer to be off welfare, would prefer to be working out of the house if only this nation of ours had taken the proper steps some time ago to ensure adequate child care service is available. We must begin to make that child care spacing available for these women.
I would like to propose that the Prime Minister or the federal government before long convene a national conference on the elimination of child poverty, inviting first and foremost the provincial governments because much of the responsibility as we know in this federal constitution of ours to deal with this problem resides with the provinces. Also invited should be municipalities to send delegates, volunteer agencies, the trade union movement, chambers of commerce, service clubs and poor peoples' representatives themselves.
There should be a national effort to talk about and understand the gravity of the problem and to understand that things can be done. Tliis conference should be called. In my view such a grand coalition that could be brought together should not be a one-shot deal, but it should obligate itself to meet on an annual basis to establish targets. I am aware we cannot do this overnight, as I am aware if we begin to spend money now and target spending to overcome the disgrace of national poverty
for children certain other priorities would have to be set aside. No serious man or woman in political life can escape from that. I am aware that it cannot be done overnight and without some sacrifice in some other domain, but by God I am saying we should now organize our political community like we have never done before. This can be done by bringing in groups that have not been involved before, setting out a national target, and monitoring it on an annual basis until we eliminate child poverty in this country.
I want to conclude with these observations. Whatever their philosophical basis, whether Canadians are Conservatives, Liberals or New Democrats, I know there is not the slightest bit of difference in terms of their commitment to the well-being of children. However else we may differ on other political matters, and the differences are real and serious, on this issue there is no difference on the commitment to overcome child poverty. I believe there would be no difference about that goal.
I think that if we speak to all of Canada and if all Parties took this on, we could get a response. I am convinced that a great attempt to mobilize the energy and effective imagination of Canadians would meet with a great response from the people of Canada. We have the resources. We have the ability. We have done it before on pensions. We have done it before on medicare. What we need now is to demonstrate the same will concerning the needs of our children.
For the sake of our children, let us find that same spirit of reform, of hope, of courage, of tenacious intelligence that has led this nation of ours to great accomplishments in the past. Native leaders in this Shibogama Tribal Council area are discouraged by the increase in suicides among their young people. They are most concerned with the increasing number of aboriginal youth who turn to suicide as a way of solving their problems.

Mr. Speaker, after listening very carefully to Hon. Members whose speeches reflected widely divergent opinions; after reading Bill C-43, an Act respecting abortion, a subject that has been extremely controversial for many years; after long discussions with many of my constituents in Ahuntsic, people whose opinions are varied and diverse; after a thorough study of the impact on abortion of our society and the moral, ethical, social, economic and demographic aspects of this issue, one which compels Canadians to examine their democratic conscience as well as their moral values; and after consulting experts on the subject such as physicians, legislators, lawyers, priests and ministers, Catholics, those of the Orthodox faith, Protestants and atheists, today, Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to give my opinion of this bill, and be as objective as I can.
First of all, I would like to say that as a Member of Parliament, a woman and former nurse, in other words, someone with a respect for life, I will vote in favour of this bill which provides a judicious and clear response to all the concerns and questions I may have had since the debate started in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, my support for Bill C-43 is not just a matter of subjective
Government Orders
emotion and deep-seated feeling, it is a reasoned and rational decision.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, coming as it does after the Supreme Court's judgment in the Morgentaler case in January 1988, is intended to fill a legal vacuum, in response to demands by Canada's modem, pluralistic society. Since our society is not monolithic, its members holding various beliefs and views, it was imperative that this legislation should strike a balance between women's constitutional rights and society's interest in protecting the foetus. This means, Mr. Speaker, that these two fundamental rights are entirely compatible: the right of the woman to control her own body and her own destiny, and that of the foetus which, although unfortunately, it has yet to be recognized by the Supreme Court, is nevertheless a moral value that no normal society would be able to reject indefinitely.
Mr. Speaker, at a time when legislators, human rights activists and even the United Nations are talking about children's rights, minority rights and women is rights, a perverse selfishness that stifles all feelings of compassion and generosity leads us to ignore the rights of the foetus which is, at whatever stage of its development- embryology and the latest scientific techniques such as ultrasound prove it-a being in essence, in other words, a human being that is genetically alive. To talk about the rights of this fragile and voiceless being is, according to some people, tantamount to preaching in the wilderness and having opinions that are reactionary and outdated.
If, as these modernists claim, morality changes as new scientific discoveries are made, then I say those who speak for the unborn are pioneers, working towards a future where the rights of all will be respected, including the rights of the foetus. What future is there for a society that is unmoved by its own voluntary extinction and does not fight for its survival? What future is there for a country that, if it does not pass laws on such an essential issue, is doomed to a geometrical decline in its birth rate? The primary objective of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to reconcile two fundamental rights that are complementary and equal.
The second objective of this legislation is to provide fair and reasonable access to abortion, while preventing abuse and charlatanism. We know that many women, especially young women, left to themselves, accept willingly or are forced into some abortion practices that endanger their own physical and psychological health. For all the reasons that have already been given, abor-

Government Orders
tion must not be a form of birth control. It is therefore our duty as a responsible government to protect the life and health of the women in our country. This bill does so by removing several administrative obstacles, such as therapeutic abortion committees. These took a long time to make a final decision and thus prevented women from fully exercising their right to a legal abortion, thereby infringing on their physical and psychological health.
But, as I see it, Mr. Speaker, what is most important and what convinced me that this bill is positive and fair is the doctor's involvement in this big decision. For me, this is not paternalistic; the doctor will not tell the woman in an authoritarian way what choice or decision to make. Whatever decision she makes, she will always need to call on a doctor to perform an abortion and thus abortion is first and foremost a medical procedure. Who, Mr. Speaker, is in a better position than the doctor, with his scientific knowledge, professional ethics and practice, to make a definite decision that will take into account the woman's health, the foetus' rights and society's responsibilities?
Furthermore, the doctor who performs an abortion as prescribed by law for medical reasons related to physical, mental and psychological health is, according to the generally recognized standards of his profession, responsible for monitoring the woman after her abortion. He is inevitably involved and takes part in this process, like it or not. The bill simply confirms his deep involvement in providing an abortion. He is not acting as a moral adviser but as a qualified professional trained to make such a dicision. On Monday, October 30, 1989, the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader raised as a point of order several questions regarding the conduct of business on a supply day.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and several others offered comments on these questions. I want to thank members for their contributions to this debate on an interesting procedural matter. I have considered the matter carefully and am now prepared to respond.

The first question asked by the parliamentary secretary was whether it was necessary for the government to designate a supply day before the opposition can give notice of a motion they want debated. The parliamentary Secretary maintained that it was a necessary precondition. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands suggested that in this specific case it was not necessary and that, in any case, it had been done in anticipation of Friday being a votable supply day.

According to our rules and practice, the purpose of notice is to give warning to the House of an item of business that might be raised for debate. The notice does not necessarily mean that the item will actually be debated or that it will be debated any time soon.

December 7, 1989
Speaker's Ruling
The Order Paper contains numerous items for which notice has been given but which have not yet been debated. The parliamentary secretary suggested that proceedings on supply days are different.
While I agree that certain aspects of supply have a character distinct from other proceedings, it seems to me that unless the rules on supply are explicit, the usual practices should be followed. This is the case with notice.
It is competent for any opposition member to file a motion that might be debated on a supply day. Normally what happens is that members file supply day motions at the latest possible moment after a day has been designated by the government, but this does not preclude the right to give notice of the supply motion well in advance of a supply day. Indeed this has happened.
In 1982 a supply day motion originally filed on February 11 remained on the Notice Paper for almost six weeks and through three supply days before being taken up on the final allotted day in the supply period ending late in March. While it may be unusual to have the supply day motion filed well in advance of a designated day, it is not prohibited by either our rules or our practice.
As his second point, the parliamentary secretary asked a question relating to the intent of Standing Order 81(12)(c), which gives the Speaker the power to select opposition motions on allotted days when notice has been given of more than one. He felt that the idea behind this Standing Order was to cover those situations where motions had been put on notice by both of the opposition parties, but that it was not the intention that one party could put down more than one notice or the same notice but in the name of another hon. member.
The recognition of two opposition parties is not explicitly contemplated in the Standing Orders. Speakers in the past have indicated that they have selected motions with a view to the proportional balance of the opposition parties in the House, but this does not necessarily address the entire issue of selection.
Other considerations might need to be taken into account, particularly in instances where there are several notices, some of which could be submitted by members of the same party. The date of the notice, the sponsor of the motion, the subject matter raised and whether the
motion is votable or not can be weighed by the Speaker when making a final decision.
I would agree with the parliamentary secretary that the political parties are factored into any decision, but I would have to add that it is not the only criterion used nor is it necessarily the most important one and, as I have stated earlier, there is nothing in the Standing Orders which in any way limits the number of notices which may be given.

The third question of the parliamentary secretary has to do with the withdrawal of a notice of motion. The parliamentary secretary asks if it is in order "for any or all notices for such motions to be withdrawn without the consent of the House." The simple answer to this question is yes. As long as a motion has not been proposed to the House, as long as the House is not properly seized of the motion, then it is still only a notice and it remains possible for the sponsor to secure its withdrawal unilaterally. The sponsor of the notice of motion could even refuse to move it when the order is called and it would be dropped. Once it is in the possession of the House, however, the motion becomes the property of the House and it is the House which must then consent to the motion being withdrawn from further consideration or possible decision.
The authorities are clear on this. Beauchesne, Bouri-not and May all confirm that members retain the right to withdraw notices of motions before they have been proposed to the House. See, for example, Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 398 on page 144 and Bourinot Fourth Edition, page 296 where one reads:
A notice of motion may be withdrawn at any time by the member
upon merely notifying the Clerk of the House of his desire so to do.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to speak in support of this motion introduced by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West and seconded by the hon. member for Davenport, providing that the government should consider introducing legislation to fully protect the Canadian environment through the institution of mandatory environment impact assessment procedures which would allow for assessments prior to the installations, public or private, of projects which may prove to be potentially damaging to the environment.

The state of the environment, especially the rate at which it changes, is of fundamental importance to a nation's long-term well-being. Canadians have benefited greatly from Canada's vast natural resources. Forests, fisheries, agriculture, fur-bearing animals and minerals have been the backbone of Canada's economic development.
But the desire for continuous improvements in the economic standard of living has not, until recently, been accompanied by a sufficient awareness of some serious adverse environmental effects of economic development. As prominent environmentalist, David Suzuki, points out, economic growth has become an end in itself, "a mindless goal that is sought by every country in the world and the very measure of progress". We must reverse this insane idea that growth is of vital necessity if we really want to preserve something for future generations, to meet their needs, the essence of sustainable development.
December 7, 1989

It is this irrational and self-destructive use of economic growth as the overriding criterion of national well-being that is the number one obstacle which prevents us from being able to successfully address our environmental problems today. But there are other obstacles.

Another obstacle which prevents us from being able to develop a coherent and effective strategic plan to protect our environment is the institutional rigidity of our political system. Decisions are made too often for shortterm political gain rather than for long-term environmental benefit.
Finally, we are trying to clean up and protect the environment with ad hoc, linear methods that are ineffective given the cumulative, synergistic nature of the problem. We deal with the effects rather than causes, with symptomatic treatment rather than definitive cures or prevention.
Because environmental impact assessment procedures are a preventive tool, they are an essential element in an effective environmental strategy. This is why I support this motion.
Canada is a democratic federation operating in a mixed economy. Hence, management and control of resources, their uses and their by-products, is dispersed between the different levels of government and the private sector. BasePK: 3806260

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, recently Canada joined all major countries in the world as a signator to the historic UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Canada, as a result, is legally obligated to adapt our policies and our legislation to reflect this convention as it applies particularly to protect the rights of children in Canada.
This motion we are debating today, which was sponsored by the member for Mission-Coquitlam, reinforces the UN convention by advocating a bill of rights for Canadian children. I commend her for her initiative. We hope this motion will be adopted not only by this House but by all provinces and by the Government of Canada as a guideline and commitment to protect the rights of Canadian children.
When we see the plight of starving children on TV, children from Africa with their bloated bodies and eyes that we cannot bear to look into, we are moved. But do we take action?
UNICEF reported at a conference I attended last summer that 40,000 children die each day from simple childhood diseases that are preventable. The cost of curing these diseases is minimal and yet do we contribute, as citizens, to save one child?
Today it was reported on the CBC that the UN predicts 100 million children may die in the next 10 years because of lack of nutrition and neglect. It is almost unbelievable that we live in this kind of a world.
However, in our concern for the world's children we must not forget our own children in Canada. The problems of many of Canada's children are hidden behind closed doors in our cities, towns and countryside. Child poverty, child abuse and child neglect are not visible. Yet, in Canada, well over one million children live below the poverty line. Children are the fastest growing users of food banks in this country.
Many of these children are disadvantaged from birth. Child mortality rates are twice as high in poor households as in the rest of the country. Babies are born underweight and face medical complications because of their mothers' poor nutrition during pregnancy. Young brains, as a result, do not develop and progress in school is difficult. Poor kids face a high dropout rate in high school, further limiting their options. Many become

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
homeless street kids in their teens, with all the dangers that lifestyle entails. Verbal, physical and sexual abuse of children also are on the rise. Many children who are sexually abused grow up to become prostitutes and patients in psychiatric hospitals, and we viewed this recently, in dramatic terms, in documentaries on television.
Canada was a signator to the UN convention on the rights of the child and we are morally bound to adhere to its precepts. Article 27 of this convention states that as a member nation we, as a signator, must ensure a standard of living adequate for children's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development.
While parents have the primary responsibility to provide security of life for their children, this is often not within their financial capacities. This means that where there are difficulties and where incomes are inadequate in families-and there are many, many of these, one in four children are in families who are in this situation- the state must supplement incomes and provide support programs. But we are not doing that in an adequate way. Sure, we have token welfare programs, but they are far below the minimum standard that is needed to sustain a family with young children.
I think that this government has short-changed us. Our children surely are our future, and our future is in trouble. Our society creates child poverty and neglect because it is based on inequalities. Women are left alone to raise children, without adequate incomes and without opportunities for independence in the future. Many parents are unemployed or underemployed. Housing is unaffordable for many young families today.
Our Conservative government leaves people at the mercy of the market-place where corporations reap profits while people lose jobs, and of course children suffer. Instead of improving social security and family benefits, the government's tax policies have increased the burden on low-income people.
What can we do to ensure that the rights of children are protected in Canada? We need a policy of full employment so that parents will be guaranteed a job with pay equity and parental leave provisions and affordable, quality child care. We need a children's bill of rights that
will be enforced by governments, and by the federal government in particular.
I support the motion of my hon. colleague for Mission-Coquitlam that this government should begin negotiating with the provinces to provide a children's bill of rights which will standardize laws throughout Canada. I also support her motion that this bill of rights should include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
Why do we as Canadians and as world citizens tolerate the hardship that so many of our children are experiencing?

Mr. Speaker, if I may I would like very briefly to direct some remarks toward the proposed amendment.
Let me begin by saying, as I have tried to tell the House before, there comes a time in labour-management disputes when the matters at issue go beyond immediate concerns of that labour dispute and affect the broad public interest. That has been recognized in this House of Commons and in this Parliament of Canada time and time again. It has not been with any relish. Nobody enjoys back to work legislation. At some time Parliament has to accept its responsibility to the general public and introduce legislation.
May I indicate to the House some remarks made by a former Liberal cabinet minister who this very day sits in the House of Commons representing Papineau-Saint-Michel. He said it very well back on October 17, 1978 when he said in this House of Commons:
Unfortunately, however, there are times and situations when the spirit of compromise and the demonstration of good faith so necessary on the part of all concerned are found wanting. In such circumstances the federal government, as custodian of the economy and protector of the public interest, must assume its responsibility.
That is the very case in which back to work legislation is introduced into the House of Commons-not to anybody's particular desire but as a way to protect the public interest and terminate a labour-management dispute and bring about a settlement.
The question that is posed by the amendment may be: "How do you bring about a settlement?" Obviously, you want to do it in the fairest and most expeditious way possible. That was the purpose of naming the chairpersons of those two
conciliation boards, as explained by the minister and by his officials.
If it would serve the purposes of settlement to change that, I am sure there would be a disposition to make that change. But that disposition has to be evidenced, not by members opposite. They represent their constituencies. This is a bargaining situation. We have the Public Service Alliance on the one hand, the Treasury Board on the other. Who speaks for the Public Service Alliance? Not the member from Halifax, not the member from Ottawa West, not the member from Saskatoon-Dundum. If the officials of the Public Service Alliance of Canada want specific changes made, they can speak in the negotiation that the President of the Treasury Board offered them in this House. Stay at the table and those changes can be negotiated, but not in debate in the House of Commons.
Surely the member from Ottawa West knows that that is not the way you resolve a labour-management dispute. You cannot resolve it on the floor of the House of Commons. It has to be resolved by the parties.
If the members want to serve a useful purpose in the resolution of this labour-management dispute, they should go back to the people they represent and urge them to sit at the table with the appropriate officials of the Public Service Alliance and of the Treasury Board and resolve these matters.
We are here to reflect the will of the parties once that will, that consensus, that agreement is achieved. I do not think, certainly speaking for the President of the Treasury Board, that his concerns are any more than I have stated. If there is a will on behalf of the bargaining parties to come to some agreement, the net agreement can be reflected in the legislation. Madam Speaker, I must say that I rise today with great difficulty to discuss Bill C-28 or, more important, the closure that comes with it. As a new member of Parliament I have a lot of difficulty, as do a lot of members, trying to figure out the procedures of the House. When we first came to the House we were told that this was one of the procedures that would not be used very often. I recall the discussion we had with the Whip who told us not to be too worried about closure, that it only happened once in a while.
All of a sudden I notice that closure takes place almost every day in the House. I am getting to know the rules quite well and understand the procedures, but I want to talk a bit about closure and about what this House is supposed to be for. I think it would be important in this debate for members opposite to pay a little attention so they could understand my reasons for thinking why they are here and why they were elected by their constituents.
I was elected to voice my opinion on behalf of the people of Kenora-Rainy River. When I return to the riding on weekends and when the House is not sitting, on a regular basis the people of Kenora-Rainy River give me their input on what is important to the country and what direction they want us to go.
One thing that really bothers me is the fact that on all bills that we have debated closure, in particular, nobody on the other side gets up to represent their constituents. I find that deplorable. It is one thing to vote with the government side because you are a member of the government; "Hold your nose", as they say, and "go ahead and do it".
It is difficult in our party system to vote against your own party. That is understandable. I think people can understand that, but they do not understand when people come to the House, sit here all day long-or in this case for an hour-and not rise once to defend the reason closure is in place, to defend the reason this particular amendment of Bill C-28 is taking place. If

they agree with closure, then let us change the procedures of the House so that we only debate for an hour and, if that is acceptable to Canadians, then so be it. However if it is not, then we should stop using this particular procedure which was put on the books for purposes of emergencies.
This is not a great emergency. I do not see any seniors outside saying: "Hurry up and put this in place. I can hardly wait to have my hard earned funds taxed back and clawed back as quickly as I can, so get on with it!" I think that is something that the members opposite should pay close attention to.
The people back home are starting to pay closer attention to what the Conservative members are doing. One thing they must be asking themselves over and over again is: "Who is speaking for me? Who is speaking out? Why are they not saying what they think?" If they really believe that this is the way to go for the future, then by all means they should be standing up in their place and doing that.
Another thing that we should touch on is: What does closure really mean? You close the door, the window, or perhaps the lid on something that is open. Whether it be in the fridge or in the cupboard closure means basically that. You put a stop to something. The environmental aspects of closing a door is that you do not want the cold air to come in or, for that matter, they might not want the fresh air to come in.
What we are seeing here with members opposite is that they are putting closure in place because they do not want us as opposition members to use our abilities to speak in the House and to tell the people of Canada what is taking place. That is a very dangerous precedent. To continue doing that on a regular basis really undermines democracy and the ability to speak our minds whether or not they agree with it. Really, it does not make any difference whether they completely agree with my point of view. In this country I have the ability to speak for the people I represent.
Another thing I have noticed is that the government opposite does not like the members of the opposition, members of the Liberal Party in particular, to speak
about the clawback. In essence, they believe that we do not know what we are talking about.
Today I have prepared some quotes we have heard over and over again to make members opposite more aware that aside from the seniors we are not the only ones who are saying it is not good. There are other people who have a common voice, a lot of exposure, and are well respected members of Canadian society speaking on this issue. I think the government should pay closer attention to that.
One Voice, the Canadian seniors network states: "History will remember the clawback as the end of universality, not for its drop in the deficit bucket".
Then there is Don McGillivray, our good friend from The Ottawa Citizen who states: "The policy pretends to continue universality, but in fact cancels it".
Then there is Hugh Winsor of The Globe and Mail of all places who states: "If, as Mr. Mulroney subsequently admitted, tampering in the indexation was wrong in 1985, attempting the same thing with the threshold levels is wrong in 1989".
Leonard Shifrin, in an article published in The Ottawa Citizen states that the finance minister "proceeded to undermine the universality of family allowances and old age pensions".
A report from the National Council of Welfare states: "A social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them all back from some recipients is not universal".
We are not the only ones in Canada who are disappointed that what this government is doing through the back door in a sneaky way is moving away from universality. What it is doing is changing the way we look at ourselves. That is something that should be heavily debated, not something that should be just fed in there very quickly.

I do not want to have to contend with the braying of the untutored and the uncaring.
I quote now from the Kirby task force report. Mr. Kirby was appointed by the last Liberal government to look at the crisis it created with interest rates and double digit inflation. What did he recommend? He recommended enterprise allocations. Fifty-one of these 57 recommendations were approved. One of them was enterprise allocations or company quotas to the large offshore companies.
He said in his report that the northern cod quota was projected to reach 380,000 tonnes by 1987. What was it in actual fact in 1987? It was considerably less than that. In 1987 the actual total allowable catch was 256,000 tonnes, not 380,000 tonnes. Even the great Kirby was far out in his projections.
Then there was an Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act. What was the purpose given in the legislation? To facilitate the development of viable Atlantic fisheries that are competitive and privately owned through the restructuring of fishery enterprises. That was what the last government did. The last government put over $300

million into these companies-Fishery Products and National Sea they eventually became. It put $300 million into companies.
It was the one who introduced the big company solution of 1983, which members opposite now decry and would they blame us if we give these companies any understanding at all or try to see that they remain viable economic units. There is nothing but scorn from the other side. These are the companies created by the big company solution, the Liberal solution of 1983. It was their restructuring which did nothing for the smaller companies and the inshore sector.
This time that is not the route we are going. We are going the route of helping the communities. We are going the route of helping the people and helping the fishermen of Atlantic Canada.
We are looking at two things-a long-term solution which was never attempted by the last government. That involves the restructuring in Newfoundland and Labrador of our fishery. Just listen to these figures and give some thought to what they reveal.
Fishing contributes 6 per cent only to the Newfoundland Gross Domestic Product but 25 per cent to total employment. Is it any wonder that our people who are in the fishery and in fish processing have only low incomes to look to?
The average Saskatchewan farm family in 1986 had an income of $32,000-34 per cent from farming, 40 per cent from other employment earnings, nothing from UI and 26 per cent from other sources.
The average Atlantic farm family had an income of $33,750.
The average Nova Scotia fishing family had an income of $35,000-53 per cent from fishing, 25 per cent from employment earnings, 16 per cent from UI and 6 per cent from other sources.
In Newfoundland, the place that I am most concerned about, the average fishing family income in 1986 was $19,850 of which only 24 per cent came from fishing, 30 per cent from other employment earnings, 41 per cent from UI and 5 per cent from other sources.
Is this the state that we want to leave our people in who are engaged in the fishery in Newfoundland now or do we want to build a viable fishery? I opt for building a viable fishery, and that is what we are dam well going to do.
Just consider this. In 1975 we had 10,283 plant workers in the fishing plants in Newfoundland. In 1988 we had 28,446 just about triple.
In 1975 we had 15,812 part-time and full-time fishermen. In 1988 we had 29,826 full-time and part-time fishermen.
Is it any wonder that the people involved in the fishery have low average incomes with a large percentage of their income coming from UI. What can we do to change this?
There are two approaches to this problem that we are taking. One is to deal with the immediate results of plants that might have to close because there is no fish there to put through the plants.

Mr. Speaker, this government certainly has supported the needs of the Canadian agri-food industry and it has never wavered here at home or internationally.
The hon. member for Mackenzie is taking us to task for adjustments that have been made to our agricultural programs over the last year. Of course we have had to make adjustments; the changes taking place in agriculture demand it. And I can assure the hon. member that we will continue to respond to the changing agriculture environment. These adjustments to our policies and programs have been consistent with the objectives outlined in the national agriculture strategy signed by federal and provincial agriculture ministers in 1986. They are consistent with the national policy review we are currently leading.
The hon. member has suggested that our agriculture policy is authored by our international trading partners and that they are GATT driven. This is simply not the case. The government has and will continue to develop agriculture policy that meets Canadians' needs and conditions.
Yes, we have adjusted our programs in a way that also reflects our goal and approach in the MTN. This does
Adjournment Debate
not mean we have softened in the defence of our agri-food industry. We firmly maintain our right to design programs that suit Canadians' needs but are also consistent with our international obligations.
That is why Canada is working hard with other countries for international trade reform through multilateral trade negotiations. We expect all countries will agree to adjust their policies consistent with the new rules that are being negotiated. This will reduce trade distortions and lead to a fairer and more open international trading system.
I also want to assure the hon. member that this government remains committed to agriculture research in Canada. Agriculture Canada is a leader in this area with an annual research budget of $250 million. We will continue to support this activity to meet the needs of the agri-food industry.

This is also happening at the Animal Research Centre in Ottawa because industry has picked up long-term animal breeding technology developed at the centre. The arc is now moving toward the development of new technology to improve animal production. The centre is reorienting its research programs toward the key areas of safety and quality of food, animal bio-technology, animal behaviour and environmental quality. However, the centre is moving in these scientific directions at the same time as existing programs are being completed. Because of this, the centre was heading toward a serious budget overrun in this transition period and extra controls had to be imposed.
Funding to the centre has not been cut and frozen, as the hon. member has stated. Rather, expenditures are being managed and controlled within the existing budget for the remainder of the fiscal year. This is not only ensuring that the centre can continue to provide essential services but also that it has this flexibility to meet urgent needs and maintain ongoing research programs. We are trying to do the maximum research with the resources available.
This government is committed to providing the sort of agricultural policies and programs that are in tune with the needs of our agri-food industry and we will continue to adjust these policies and our programs.

Indeed, I am pleased to speak to this motion which is of vital importance to Canadians and which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider developing special initiatives, in consultation with aboriginal peoples, to respond to the serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
What is the situation for native Canadians? The situation for them, particularly the aboriginal youth, is that they are economically disadvantaged. There is discrimination, they are in poor health, social services are inadequate and hence, they suffer cultural isolation. As a consequence, they feel that they are second-class citizens.
It is particularly important that we focus on the youth because the native problems are magnified for them. They encounter tremendous obstacles, such as completing their education, finding a job, trying to handle or prevent pre-marital pregnancies, alcohol and drug abuse, suicide and problems with the justice system.
Private Members' Business
Only recently we have seen the report of the royal commission on the Marshall inquiry when Canadians have been told that, in fact, racial discrimination towards aboriginal people does exist. It is a sad state, Mr. Speaker.
The second reason why we should focus on the aboriginal youth is because the birth rate for native people is higher than for non-native Canadians. As a consequence, the aboriginal youth constitute a significant proportion of our native population. Therefore, their needs become greater and I should say quickly that their needs are truly urgent.
As a result of all of these things, we can anticipate increased family tensions and one does not have to quote any more statistics, because if there is higher unemployment for them, alcohol abuse, and drug problems, obviously the suicide problem will impact on the instability of the family. This must be addressed and must be addressed with initiatives, as indicated by the motion proposed.
The three specific areas that we are trying to address with this particular motion are health, education and employment. It is known that poverty, drug abuse, alcohol abuse, and geographic isolation would magnify any health problem any Canadian citizen would have. Because these problems are high among our native youth it should follow that they face these problems much more than the non-native Canadians.
The problem of their nutrition is also important. Just a few days ago my colleague from Nunatsiaq indicated to this House how, with the GST, the prices of food would increase in his part of the country. When the cost of food increases it should follow that access to them could be hindered and that would lead, or could lead, to malnutrition.
A University of Toronto study recently indicated that Indians on two northern Ontario reserves are twice as likely as an average Canadian to have a physical disability such as hearing, speaking and even seeing. This is as a consequence of poor living conditions and inadequacy of medical treatment and specialized medical services.
At one time the federal government agreed to transfer health care services to native control, but it was only a partial solution because the transfer of control was mainly administrative and the determination of the level

of services that ought to be provided for native people was not given to them.
The second area is education. It is known that the schools are lacking in research. Not only are the schools lacking but the equipment for these schools is lacking. As well, the number of qualified teachers and teachers familiar with the cultural, language and sensitivity of native youth is absent.
On many reserves schools offer education only to a grade eight level. How can we expect them in the future to be as good as we are? That ought to be our challenge as we ought to provide for them as good an education as any other Canadian across the country. When the drop-out rate is very high, when only about 7 per cent of them-those between the ages of 20 and 24-are able to attend university levels, there is something wrong with our system in this country.
The availability of the services and the availability of opportunities ought to be open to all. Since education is a necessary tool to break the cycle of dependency, when that education is not attainable, then the dependency of our native population will continue to be present and that, of course, does not speak well for our country.
Hence, aboriginal people need a fully-integrated aboriginal education system that would care for and teach native children from a native perspective. Mr. Speaker, I pleased to speak to the motion this afternoon. We are all aware of the problems Canadian grain farmers face. The financial squeeze which began gripping farmers in the middle of the decade has not yet loosened. Export subsidy battles fought by others on the world grain markets have depressed the prices Canadian farmers get for their grain. Until there is some further progress made in the trade talks through the GATT, or unless there are production problems in major grain growing regions, the situation will remain uncertain.
In recent years dealing with problems brought on by low commodity prices has meant relying to a large extent on ad hoc government programs for support. In 1986 and 1987 the federal government provided farmers with a total of $2.1 billion through the Special Canadian Grains Program. In 1988 the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program paid out $850 million to farmers who suffered crop losses because of the severe drought.
We cannot continue to rely on ad hoc government assistance. There must be a better way in place to provide protection to grain and oilseed producers. This government has set out to find that better way. It began last year with changes to crop insurance plans. Coverage was increased in 1989. As a result of that increased coverage the revamped crop insurance programs in 1989 provided farmers with more coverage than in the previous year.
For example, the 1988 crop insurance payments for wheat on stubble in Saskatchewan ranged from about $32 to $53 an acre, depending on the risk area. In 1989, coverage for the same risk areas ranged from about $50 to $85 per acre.

February 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
In 1988, a southeastern Saskatchewan fanner, who grew a crop of wheat on summer fallow would have been eligible for about $60 an acre in crop insurance. On top of this, the same farmer would also have received about $14 an acre from the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program. The maximum coverage for that farmer would have been approximately $75 an acre.
After changes to crop insurance in 1989, that same farmer would have been eligible for about $94 an acre from crop insurance alone. Producers in Alberta and Manitoba were also eligible for more coverage through crop insurance alone in 1989 than they were able to collect from drought assistance and crop insurance in 1988.
The changes to crop insurance protection was a first step. Now this government is moving on the development of a national safety net program for all grain and oilseed producers. It seems inappropriate at this time to be tinkering with individual programs like the WGSA and the ASA. We have to look at this issue in a broader context.
At the National Agri-Food Policy Conference in Ottawa in December, it was agreed there is an urgent need to help develop a national safety net program that is fair to all grain and oilseed producers. Work on this issue is being undertaken as part of the federal government's national agricultural policy review. It was announced at the conference that the national grains bureau in Winnipeg would take the lead in working to develop a national grain safety net program.
This task will include the involvement of provincial governments and those industry representatives in developing a proposal. Meetings are under way this month. It is expected that a proposal should be ready by late spring with enabling legislation developed by December 1990.
The federal government is moving quickly on this issue. The farm income problems projected for the next year must be taken into account. There is also a need to ensure that action taken now is in line with the longer term goals as safety nets are developed for all farmers.
Part of the review, of course, is the examination of existing safety net programs. The advisory committee of the western grain stabilization program has been asked
to examine issues surrounding the potential transition of the WGSA to a more comprehensive safety net program.
This government is moving on the issue. In fact, progress has been made. The existing federal-provincial working group on safety nets is continuing the work it began in 1988. Its key objective is to develop a long term comprehensive safety net policy for all commodities and all farmers.
A series of regional meetings were held during 1988 among all farm leaders across Canada and government to help identify the problems which exist with existing safety net programs and determine the direction that would be taken for agriculture in the future.

The work of the National Grains Bureau on safety nets is continuing. Continued discussion with farm leaders across Canada with other government members is continuing to work out a program for agriculture. As a government we are working out a comprehensive program which is fair to all producers across Canada. It will have a sound financial base for Canadian farmers which they require at this time.
This government has taken action and will continue to take action to ensure that agriculture is protected across this great land. We feel that it is appropriate for this government to continue to discuss with the farm leaders the future of agriculture, combining crop insurance and some safety net programs. We are continuing working with that to develop protection for producers.

exists. It allows members of Parliament to make a decision according to his or her own conscience whether or not they will present a petition with which they agree, present a petition with which they disagree and believe in their own conscience it is their duty to do so, or feel so strongly opposed to the subject matter in question as to refuse to present the petition altogether.

In similar manner, rules are designed, I would argue, to reflect that in regard to petitions. In other words, we can make those kinds of decisions of conscience to which I was referring a while ago.
Our petition form, Mr. Speaker, which our rules provide for us, refers to the ancient and undoubted right to petition Parliament. Clearly, what is insinuated here is if a person has a right to petition Parliament, obviously Parliament has an obligation to receive the petition, and in order for Parliament to have that obligation to receive it, I think one can safely deduce that the parliamentarian in question has the same duty to present the petition in question.
I have in the past presented petitions with which I disagreed. In the Ontario legislature, where I had the honour and privilege of serving prior to coming to this House, I have upon occasion stated publicly while presenting a petition, albeit briefly and without presenting argument, that I was presenting a petition signed by so many constituents with whom I disagreed, and so on, and described the petition. I did not make an argument as to why I disagreed with it but merely stated so in one or two words. The point is that I felt this was a happy medium between my fulfilling my duty as a member of Parliament on the one hand and, of course, making it quite clear that I did not necessarily endorse the petition that I was presenting.
That, I believe, is the issue before us today; whether or not it is our duty to present petitions. I do not suppose we will solve that situation today, but I would argue that perhaps we should not, perhaps that issue should be left to the conscience of individual members.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity this afternoon of taking part in this veiy significant debate. It is unfortunate that the debate is in such a negative tone. I think that we in Canada have made real progress in the last few years in our racial relations. I say that coming from the west coast where we have had in the past very severe problems with our native Indians, the Chinese, the Japanese and the East Indians. I think matters have improved considerably, something which has been largely due to the policies of this government. However, we recognize that in Canada we still have significant problems with prejudices against minorities, whether they be racial, religious or whatever.
I would like to spend the few minutes that I have this afternoon to comment on the relationship with our native minorities. I believe that we just need to look at the Manitoba justice inquiry and also the Marshall inquiry to recognize that natives all over the country do suffer from the effects of ignorance and misunderstanding on the part of many Canadians.
Supply
We need to recognize also that these prejudices are rooted in hundreds of years of history and that to expect legislation to remove them in very short order is unrealistic. I think that it is worth while to look at some of the things that this government is doing and has done to correct that situation. We recognize that many of the problems that natives face are as a result of poverty and other social problems which our native population has to struggle against. Much needs to be done, both for our native Indians and also the Inuit.
I recognize that both of these groups of people have real hopes and ambitions just as the rest of Canadians have. The Ministers of Indian Affairs over the years have made many changes and changes will continue to be made as policies are required.
One of the major government policies that we are working on at the present time to allow the Indian population to take its rightful place in Canadian society is the promotion of self-government. We have seen, particularly in the last 10 to 15 years, the growing responsibility of the First Nations to assume responsibility for their educational, judicial, social and economic life.
Many of the disadvantages such as poverty are diminishing. As self-reliance and independence become the norm for our native people and the Inuit of Canada, Canadians are seeing the emergence of strong, dynamic partners in our economy, our cultural diversity and prosperity. Much evidence of our efforts to assist the native people can be seen and is becoming more obvious each year.
For example, there is the native justice system. As I mentioned earlier, this is a question which preoccupies all of us in the light of recent events in Canada. There was a federal task force conducted just recently on the question of reserve policing services. It has been shown that native communities are better served by law enforcement based on an understanding of the traditions and culture of these communities.
Administering the law at any time is not easy. It is important that those who are administering the law understand the cultural background of the people they are assisting.
Traditional Indian ways and practices increasingly enhance the peace and the harmony in our native communities. It is the goal of this government to

February 13, 1990
Adjournment Debate
enhance and increase the representation of native Canadians in the judicial system, as well as in the policing and legal professions. We have an example of that in our own party here in the House.
In many places in the country the number of native Indians in the prison population is entirely disproportionate to the general population. Mr. Speaker, the question which I raised had to do with the very serious problems which are affecting Atlantic Canada around the reduction of activities of National Sea Products. In the questions that I raised, I was particularly concerned with the results for the community of Canso and for the workers of National Sea within that community. There were essentially three questions which I raised.
The first question was to ask the government what it was planning to do for the future of those workers who would not benefit from jobs under the so-called saviour plan of National Sea. There was no answer to that question.
The second question was why the trade union involved representing those workers had been left out of the negotiations which had taken place. If those workers had been represented and able to put their point of view in the negotiation process, I would have thought that a much better result could have been expected. But they
February 13, 1990

were not represented. I raised the question, and once more no answer was given by the government.
Finally, I asked the government when it was going to protect workers in Atlantic Canada-and one could make the same point for workers across the country- from arbitrary plant shutdowns on the part of companies that do not take into account the serious detrimental impact on local communities which results. To that as well there was no answer provided.
The reality which results for the community of Canso, for the plant operations in that community, can be summarized in the following terms: the trawler fleet itself of National Sea has been taken out of the community, 120 jobs permanently lost; the marine division, 70 jobs permanently lost; the outside wharf work, 100 jobs permanently lost; the night shift, 175 jobs permanently lost; the meal plant, 50 jobs permanently lost.
Employees will not be entitled to severance pay because the company does not consider this a plant closure. When the plant reopens, a maximum of 150 jobs will be provided in a plant where 750 people once worked. It is true that these jobs will be shared so that there might be perhaps 300 people who benefit from the jobs themselves and the UI benefits which result from them, but there will only be 150 jobs left and fish will be trucked into Canso from other National Sea facilities in Lunenburg or Louisburg.
There is no guarantee of how much work per year will be available. For the community, this will be devastating with 600 people no longer earning an income. The result, as the union put it this proposed saviour plan, is nothing more than a band-aid resolve to a situation which required major surgery. The life of this community will be slowly sucked out.
I come from the community of Windsor, Ontario, in which the same kind of detrimental impact hit our major employer, Chrysler, in the early 1980s. The government of this country provided help. As a result of that help Chrysler revived and now provides tremendous employment possibilities throughout the community.
The community of Canso and the Atlantic fisheries communities in general deserve the same kind of generous response from the Government of Canada. It is with great disappointment that I see this government's failure

to provide that kind of generosity and care for the people of the communities of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I feel fortunate to be able to speak on the amendment which the hon. member has moved. I think it is important for us to take a look at its contents. The amendment clearly gives reasons as to why we do not want this bill to be read a second time at this point. It states that the full benefits of the increased registered retirement savings plan will only accrue to less than 1 per cent of Canadian taxpayers who earn more than $86,000 annually and that it fails to include assistance to middle and lower-income Canadians to provide stable income in their retirement years.
We have to recognize that there are a couple of trends relating to the elderly taking place in this country. I have had the opportunity in the last several weeks to attend hearings of the health and welfare committee. This committee is studying the question of aging in Canada and health services as they relate to the elderly.
The first thing that comes from all demographic information is that the number of people living to an old age in Canada is increasing dramatically. The percentage of elderly people in this country is also increasing dramatically. There are many reasons for this; improvement in health care, improvement in the workplace and changes in nutrition which have lead to an increase in the life expectancy of people. There are also some

things that have not changed dramatically. One of them is the number of elderly women who live beyond the age of 75 far outnumber the males.
I am quite interested in the question of services for the elderly because I come from a family which lives a very long time. My grandmother lived to 96, my great-aunt was 94, my mother is in her mid-eighties and has seven sisters, all of whom are alive. The youngest sister is in her late sixties and the oldest one is approaching 90 years of age.
In my father's family, my father passed away a year or two ago at the age of 93. One of the myths in the family, which we are having difficulty documenting because records in southern Russia are hard to come by, is that my great grandfather lived to be 109.
So I am vitally interested in what kinds of services are going to be available for the elderly not only in the next 20 or 30 years, but in the next 40 or 50 years. The position of the elderly in Canada has improved, particularly when it comes to income and financial security. It has improved mainly through the introduction of old age security and the Canada Pension Plan. Those are the two vehicles that Canada has used to provide universal and equitable pensions.
The only problem with the Canada Pension Plan and old age security is that initially it was intended to be extended. In the last number of years the scope of the Canada Pension Plan and the contributing factor has been diminished and the government has more and more looked on private pension plans, whether they are run by unions, by corporations and upon the RRSP program to allow the elderly to look after themselves in their old age. That is fine for people in the unionized workforce where they have good private pension plans. It has not worked for those who are in non-union or service jobs where there is no company or government-sponsored pension plans.
The RRSP has been nothing but a tax grab for the wealthy. It has nothing to do with providing universal high-calibre pensions for all Canadians.
If we look at the whole question of who contributes to RRSPs, one of the first things we will find is that not all Canadians are involved. Those on very limited incomes do not contribute. In fact, those with total incomes of less than $5,000, only .9 per cent contribute; those with incomes of $5,000 to $10,000, 3.7 per cent contribute. When we get up to those earning $25,000 nearly 33 per cent of taxpayers contribute to RRSPs. Those with incomes up to $50,000, 57 per cent contribute to RRSPs. So there is a disproportionate rate of participation in RRSP programs based on the level of income.
It is very simple. There is nothing mystical about it. The family man earning $25,000 does not have additional money that he can put in the bank for his old age regardless of whether there is a tax break or incentive to do that. The person earning over $50,000 has disposable income and he puts it aside for his old age. But he does not do it on an equal basis as the person earning $25,000. He does it with tax incentives that are much greater.
One of the real anomalies in the question of RRSPs is that if a person in the lower tax bracket of $20,000 makes a contribution of $1,000, he gets $264 back in a tax break. But if a person on a low income can afford to contribute, he or she will get $264 back for every $1,000 contributed. If a person in the highest tax bracket contributes $1,000, he or she gets $450 back. What kind of system gives the wealthy twice as much cash back as the poor?
That is the whole structure of the RRSP program. It is really an incentive for the wealthy to put aside money for their old age so they can have their retirement in comfort in Hawaii, Florida or the Bahamas. It is not designed to ensure that women who have worked all their lives at jobs paying $15,000 a year can afford to have adequate housing, food, clothing and transportation when they reach an elderly age. That is why it is so unfair.

Mr. Speaker, the hon member for Vancouver East has raised a number of very critical questions in areas that I could spend another half-hour discussing.
I want to comment on the last one particularly because it is going to be one of the major issues that this House has to deal with in the next period of time. The provincial governments can and do supplement through the Canada Assistance Plan types of income support and care programs for the elderly. I keep coming back to the fact that one of the things that we still have not fundamentally addressed in this bill is the discrepancy in income security between men and women in this country, particularly over the age of 65.
I would just like to point out a couple of figures. In 1971, the average income from all sources for men was $12,500. For women it was $6,183. By 1986, for men it had increased to $16,700, which is getting up to $1,500 a month. For women it was still just over $10,000, which is $800 a month. You cannot live in metropolitan areas and pay rent, buy food, have transportation and medical care on that level of income.

Mr. Speaker, few subjects have so aroused public opinion and stirred such individual passions as the debates over language.
But some of the finest chapters in our history were written by those who made the voice of reason prevail, who made tolerance triumph and who wrought the necessary accommodations.

Linguistic duality and the protection of minority language rights are not abstract concepts. They are given life by legislative enactments such as the Official Languages Act. They are given permanence and protection by the Constitution and they are given meaning by the national will of a generous and a tolerant people.

The rejection of minorities is an attack on the nature of Canada. When language becomes a motive for exclusion and fear, it is time for all Canadians who love their country to speak up and speak out.
There is no place in Canada for intolerance-although no one would suggest that Canada, or any other country, is absolutely free from it.
The resolution now before the House is an opportunity for all members to speak up and speak out, again, for what is best about Canada.
It is an opportunity to send an absolutely unequivocal message, again, of unity and mutual respect.
The issue before us is not bilingualism or even, despite claims to the contrary, the expense of bilingualism.
The issue before us is simple and important-the will of English- and French-speaking Canadians to continue to live together with mutual respect and fraternity, while
honouring our original undertakings to each other and to the whole nation.

It is time to refer back to some of our fundamental values and I think it is also time to try to put this entire issue in some perspective. This is not the first time nor will it be the last time that there have been misconceptions and misrepresentations on the government's policies regarding official languages.
This is not the first time nor will it be the last that certain voices have been heard alleging that the policy constitutes enforced bilingualism. Something is being "rammed down people's throats". Surely that phrase and that expression had to arise in Canada. Only in a country this prosperous and this magnificent would people have the time to worry about expressions like that. Nothing is being forced down anybody's throat, although the concept of enforced bilingualism or a double standard, one for Quebec and another for the rest of the country, has been alleged in this country from the days of the Confederation debates. There have always been voices, fortunately few and far between. But there have always been voices who have tried to trade on this kind of falsehood and distortion that fortunately has been repudiated time and time and time again by this Parliament, regardless of its composition and regardless of the government that happened to be sitting at the right of the Speaker.
There is no better way to bury these damaging misunderstandings than to recall the words of one of the original architects of the original Official Languages Act. In 1974, the Hon. Gerard Pelletier, then Minister of Communications, spoke as follows, and I quote:
-some people were surprised recently by my statement favouring the promotion of an intensely French Quebec. They thought they saw a contradiction with the federal government's official languages policy. But the efforts of the federal government in linguistic matters has always been subjected to the most absurd interpretations, the most frequent being that the ultimate objective of the Official Languages Act is to make each and every Canadian citizen bilingual. The facts are diametrically opposed to this fable: one of the effects of
February 15, 1990

this law is to permit anyone to remain unilingual, if that is his wish, in all of his relations with the Government of Canada.
If you want to be bilingual, terrific. If you want to remain unilingual and deal with the Government of Canada, the law was designed in such a way as to make sure that both sides of this great national debate and these two perceptions could be accommodated equally.
What is more appropriate for a country that values its linguistic duality and protects its linguistic minorities in an imperfect nation such as ours? While we have many advantages and many accomplishments, our imperfections show every day of the week. What would be more appropriate than to proceed on a sensitive and delicate issue along the lines that Mr. Pelletier suggested in 1974.

It is time, Mr. Speaker, to remind ourselves what it is like to be a minority and to treat minorities with the same tolerance and generosity of spirit that we would want to be treated with, if our situations were reversed.

Elow else would you treat a minority, except to ask yourselves what would it be like to be a minority and to treat the minority in exactly the same way that you would want you and your family to be treated if the situation were reversed. Surely that is a fundamental concept of social justice in this country.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to support Bill C-34, an Act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof.

The legislation establishes the Canadian Centre for Management Development as a departmental corporation focusing on the training, orientation and development of senior managers in the federal Public Service. The centre will also conduct research into issues directly
related to public sector management and develop teaching materials related to its mandate.
The bill will retain the features of the previous bill, C-148, but establishes the centre as a departmental corporation rather than as a department. As a department corporation the centre will come under the direction of a board of governors composed of chief executive officers from the private sector, senior members of the Canadian academic community and deputy heads of the federal government departments.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to pay tribute to John L. Manion, the first "Principal" of the Centre.

Mr. Manion, the first principal of the Canadian Centre for Management Development served in various functions in the Public Service for the past 37 years. As a dedicated public servant he deferred his retirement to set up this centre. His dedication included his love of helping others and of training people. He served 10 years in Manpower and 15 years in Immigration to rise to the position of Deputy Minister. It is a rare occasion indeed when a deputy minister rises from within staff. In 1979 he moved to Treasury Board before moving on to the Privy Council as senior personnel advisor. It was very fitting that John Manion be appointed as the first principal of the Canadian Centre for Management Development.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that Mr. Manion was named an Officer of the Order of Canada in 1984 and that he received the Public Service Outstanding Achievement Award in 1986. Moreover, in 1989, the Public Administration Institute of Canada awarded him the Vanier Medal in recognition of outstanding achievements and special leadership in public administration in Canada.
I would also like to pay tribute to the person who I think first had the idea of a Canadian centre for management development, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.
It was the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier who, in 1974, had the original idea. On October 31, 1977, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier introduced Bill C-304 in the House. He is the one who proposed this initiative.

In 1981, he moved a new motion which was debated in the House. Finally, in 1987, he once again had a motion put on the Order Paper to establish a national school of government administration.
On behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party, I wish to express once again our support for this initiative to establish a Canadian Centre for Management Development, an initiative that was first brought before this House by a Liberal member, the member for Ottawa- Vanier, in 1974.
The centre replaces the former Centre for Executive Development in Tourraine operated by the Public Service Commission. The 1989-90 estimates for the operation of the centre are $9.6 million compared to $4.5 million in 1988-89. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand here and speak on Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof.
In 1977, my esteemed colleague, the member for Ottawa-Vanier, proposed, as a Private Members' Bill, the establishment of, in his words, "a sort of College Canada for the administration echelons of the Government of Canada whereby the excellent reputation of the Canadian Public Service known throughout the world would be honed, polished and made even more ready to serve not only the federal government but all of the people of Canada".
The bill tabled, which would have established such a centre, died on the Order Paper at the end of that Parliament.
On April 15, 1988, Bill C-148 was first introduced to Parliament. The bill, which received unanimous approval by the House of Commons on August 25,1988, proposed to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development. Unfortunately, the thirty-third Parliament was dissolved before the bill was sent back to the House for final approval. Therefore, Bill C-148, too, died on the Order Paper.
Legislation has once again been introduced in the House of Commons that would establish this centre. The bill is a revised version of Bill C-148 and proposes that the Canadian centre be established as a departmental corporation with a board of governors rather than a department with an advisory council.
This latter fact brings up an interesting point, one that came up during the space agency centre discussions. The revised proposal would have a board of governors rather than a department with an advisory council. Whenever this happens, the fundamental issue becomes whether this type of structure undermines the accountability of the centre to the government and to Parliament.
Furthermore, the responsibilities of the proposed board of governors are not clearly defined in this bill and thus raises many questions that should be thoroughly studied. For example, what kind of power will the board be given? The principal is an ex officio voting member of the board. Does this mean that the principal can, at the

February 16, 1990
Private Members' Business
same time, report to and be accountable to the board of which he or she is a member?
Because there are no selection requirements, can the governors be selected without due regard to equitable representation of women, visible minorities, aboriginal people and persons with disabilities? There is no limit of renewal of appointments to the board by the Order in Council. Could this not lead to the institutions becoming more insular and self-perpetuating?
I am very pleased that the proposal for the idea that the member for Ottawa-Vanier made over 10 years ago looks as if it may actually have time to possibly work its way through the system. The establishment of such a centre would provide for the orientation, training and development of senior managements in the federal Public Service and the public sector, as well as research into improved public sector administration.
The establishment of the centre goes a long way to correcting some of the problems in the Public Service that were pointed out by the Auditor General this past October. In his report the Auditor General said that the management of Canada's Public Service needs a new and creative outlook, one not concerned with vicious slashes, but rather a better management. The future holds new challenges and the Public Service needs to adapt to these challenges.
Through training, orientation and development the centre will be designed to ensure that senior Public Service managers improve the analytical, creative, advisory, administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge ncessary to develop policy, respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively.
If this is to work, it is essential that we study whether the goal of the centre is to adequately prepare persons throughout the Public Service for management, including meeting employment equity objectives, and reflect adequately how management affects excellence, pride and Public Service attitudes at all levels.
I found it interesting to note that nowhere in Clause 4, which is where the objects of the centre are discussed, is there any reference to promoting the equitable representation in management of women, visible minorities, native persons and persons with disabilities. Nor does the clause refer at all to the relationship of management with employees at all levels or to the responsibility of the centre and the management category to encourage
pride, excellence and service to Canada and Canadians by all Public Service employees. It is this excellence, pride and service that the Auditor General was referring to in his report.
In conclusion, the discussion of this bill is long overdue and I am very pleased to be speaking on it. The creation of this centre will go a long way in helping our public servants maintain that excellence. The creation of the centre would enable the Public Service to recruit and maintain highly qualified individuals. At the same time the centre would enable the Public Service to address some of the problems outlined in the Auditor General's report.
The Public Service is an essential part of the functioning of this nation. I am proud to represent a riding where there are many, many public servants. All too often this government forgets or misunderstands just how important the Public Service is. The creation of the Canadian Centre for Management Development would allow the Public Service the support it requires in order for its efforts to be more effective in maintaining that excellence.
