Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a very brief contribution to the debate taking place on this important bill.
As you have heard from the previous speakers from our side, we support this bill fully in its principle on the establishment of the Canadian Centre for Management Development. We believe that the centre is and will be a worth-while venture.
My only reason for rising and saying anything today is to put on the record my objection to the way in which the government has proceeded with the establishment of this centre. It is typical of the arrogance of the government in dealing with Parliament. I have in my hand a copy of the 1989-90 estimates for the Canadian Centre for Management Development.
This centre was established by Order in Council because the government failed to get a bill through Parliament before the last general election. Now we have the spectacle of the government introducing a bill
to do what it has already done by Order in Council. It has been funding this organization for over a year. The centre has been operating. I am glad, in a way, that it is operating. Nevertheless, this is a high-handed and arrogant approach to Parliament, to establish a body by Order in Council and then march into this House with the bill and say; "Now we would like you to pass a bill to establish what we have already established".
I want to put on the record my profound objection to this procedure. The hon. member for St. John's East is wagging his finger. He should be wagging it at the Minister of Justice and the other ministers who came up with this bill. I want to state my objection for the record. If it happens again, I will make a longer and more protracted contribution, chastising the ministers for this kind of high-handed approach.

He said: Since 1984, this government has been following a consistent and comprehensive plan to ensure that Canadians can benefit from a rising standard of living and a quality of life second to none in the world.
The Budget
As a vital part of that plan, we have been striving to gain greater control over our nation's finances.
We have attached a very high priority to this objective. Because as we achieve it, we will gain greater flexibility and independence of action to meet the priorities of this government and of Canadians.
Last year I set out a five-year deficit reduction plan to achieve this objective. It was, and is, the right course to follow.
The deficit for this year is on track at $30.5 billion. But our future progress is endangered by deeply entrenched inflationary pressures.
Today I am asking Canadians to join in a broadly based program to reinforce our efforts to control government spending. This program will keep us on a track that will allow us to achieve the goals that I set out in my last budget: We will reduce the deficit to $28.5 billion this next fiscal year; We will cut it in half to $14 billion in three more years; and, We will reduce it further to $10 billion in the year after that.
This will mean that within five years the government will begin to buy back its bonds and Treasury bills. The country will be on a clear path of substantially reducing the burden of debt.
Last year I said that for every dollar the government collects, the interest on our debt was 35 cents and rising. That is money we can not use now to get taxes down or to address priorities such as environmental protection, research and development and skills training. We must pay those interest costs. In this budget I will show how, over the next five years, we can reduce that 35 cents to 26 cents-and keep it going down.

The Budget

Reducing the federal deficit will help ease inflationary pressures. That will help reduce interest rates.
Reducing the federal deficit will reduce Canada's reliance on foreign lenders. It will strengthen our sovereignty as a nation.
These are all powerful reasons for holding to the plan we started in 1984.

We have reduced the size of the public service by 12,000. The public service today is the same size as in 1973, despite the fact that Canada's population has increased by about one-fifth. Overall, spending on government operations is less now than it was in 1984.
When we first came to office, the federal government was spending $16 billion more on programs-everything except our interest costs-than it collected in revenues. Today our program spending is $9 billion less than revenues. We have turned an operating deficit into an operating surplus-a turnaround of $25 billion in just five years. And 70 per cent of this progress results from expenditure restraint. To achieve that progress, we have reduced program spending as a share of the economy to the lowest level in almost 20 years.

And I will tell you about your debt, the $200 billion debt you left us in 1984-85. I suppose you knew that when you borrow money, you have to pay interest. Everybody knows that borrowing involves

March 5, 1990
The Budget
paying interest. And before you borrow, you make sure you can meet your payments.
And now going back to the Liberal legacy of $199 billion at the end of the 1984-85. The Government of the day had therefore completely lost control over its spending and, as I said earlier, seemed unaware of the impact interest payments on its huge indebtedness would have on future administrations.
The interests which the Government must pay on this debt-I hope my colleagues opposite are listening-account for the deficit of some $30 billion which it has declared year in year out since 1986. Without this debt, Mr. Speaker, Canada would have no deficit and could even declare a surplus. In other words, we collect enough taxes to pay for absolutely all the services provided by the Government. Our deficits only represent the interests on the debt. Which means that the operating deficit of $16 billion in 1984-85 was eliminated when we took over. The very first year, the Minister of Finance showed enough restrain to achieve a reduction in expenditures in real terms. Since then, the increase has varied between 2 and 2.5 per cent, a significant change compared with the previous years.
Our friends opposite are blaming us for allowing the national debt to grow to apocalyptic proportions. It is like the pot calling the kettle black. We are forced to pay the interests on the debt which the Trudeau Government accumulated during its last ten years of tenure and that is the reason why we must continue in this direction and keep the situation under control. As future progress will be seriously compromised by inflationary economic pressures, we feel we must continue to limit public spending, something for which we need the support of all Canadians. Interest payments on the national debt are still the main component of our deficit and these budget measures will enable us to cut it down to $28.5 billion next year. By maintaining our program we expect to reduce the deficit to $14 billion over the next three years and to $10 billion in the fifth year. This means that in five years the government will begin to buy back its outstanding bonds and treasury bills and that the country will be well on its way towards a significant reduction in the national debt load.
The lower deficit will contribute to reduce inflation and that in turn will bring interests down. This is something for which the opposition parties have been clamouring for quite some time, but then it is due to the problems they left us with. A reduced deficit will make Canada less reliant on foreign lenders, thereby shoring up our national independence.
Canadians made it quite clear in recent months that they expected lower public outlays rather than higher taxes. Their message got through to the Minister of Finance and this is why his latest budget reflects this new trend.
The two-year expenditure control program will affect all areas of government spending, excepting of course income support programs for seniors, families and veterans as well as unemployment insurance and the equalization program and the Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower-revenue provinces.
The growth of expenditures for some programs will be capped at 5 per cent for the next two years. These programs relate to science and technology as well as to native and Inuit people. Opposition members describe this as a catastrophe, yet expenditures will rise by up to 5 per cent.
This applies as well to the Canada Assistance Plan for the provinces that do not receive equalization payments and of course also to defence and official development assistance.
Some programs will be frozen for two years. These programs concern established program financing per capita, tax transfers on the income of utilities, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Telefilm Canada, the Export Development Corporation and Marine Atlantic.
Some programs were reduced like the Department of the Secretary of State, small craft harbours and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
We also eliminated some projects such as OSLO, for the oil sands in northeastern Alberta, a saving of about $650 million, the Polar 8 icebreaker project, for a direct saving of $84 million in 1990-91 and $62 million in 1991-92.
We also eliminated the mining exploration incentive program. This measure should save us $50 million in 1990-91 and $125 million in 1991-92.

On Tuesday, January 23, 1990, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier rose on a point of order to express concerns about the operation of certain aspects of Standing Order 52, which is, of course, the Standing Order pertaining to emergency debates. In the ensuing
March 6, 1990

procedural discussion, the Chair heard comment from the hon. member from Kamloops, from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader and from the hon. member from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
[English\
At issue was the disposition of a number of applications for emergency debates of which notice had been given for the previous day, Monday, January 22, 1990. Members had been precluded from proceeding with these applications on that Monday because the House adopted a motion to move to Orders of the Day.
In the spirit of co-operation which sometimes prevails in this place it was agreed that those applications would be deemed to be before the House the following day. They were dealt with on Thesday, January 23, on that basis. That agreement was made subject to the express proviso that it not constitute a precedent.
The Chair undertook to reflect upon the interpretation to be accorded to this aspect of Standing Order 52 and to deal with the intricacies of the procedural matter at another time. The Chair is now prepared to share with the House the results of that consideration.

Hon. members are all familiar with the provisions of Standing Order 52, by which a member may seek permission to move the adjournment of the House in order to debate a "specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration". These emergency debates as they are known are held only when a number of hurdles as spelled out in Standing Order 52 have been crossed. In particular, Standing Order 52 (2) provides that any member wishing to move the adjournment of the House under the terms of this Standing Order must give to the Speaker, at least one hour before raising it in the House, a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed.

The items of concern addressed in the procedural exchange on this issue may be conveniently and fairly, I believe, summarized as follows.
First, concern was expressed that when a motion to move to Orders of the Day pre-empts reaching that point in Routine Proceedings at which leave to seek an
Routine Proceedings
emergency debate may be sought, the system is then short-circuited and the opportunity to present an application is not protected.
Second, it was contended that any notices to the Speaker requesting an emergency debate which are precluded from being presented on a given day should be held over and called on the next day when applications pursuant to Standing Order 52 would normally be reached.
In response to the first point I think it should be emphasized that the decision to move to Orders of the Day is one which is made by the House usually on the basis of a recorded division, presumably with full knowledge of the consequences, whatever they may be, of doing so. That being so I do not think it incumbent upon the Chair to second guess the decision of the House and its ramifications, and I would decline any invitation to do so.
As to whether notices of intention to request an emergency debate should be held over and called at the first opportunity, I have severe reservations in this regard.
The specific and important matters requiring urgent consideration, according to Standing Order 52(1), call by definition for immediate action or decision or attention. If that immediate attention is not accorded, it stands to reason that the nature of the matter may change. A delay of even 24 hours may serve either to diffuse or escalate the situation so that it is no longer an emergency or, conversely, it is even more critical. For this reason the Chair is reluctant to institute what would be a new practice of holding over such notices.
This reluctance is enforced by the consciousness that were notices to be held over, some hon. members may for a variety of valid reasons not be prepared to proceed with them on a subsequent occasion.
Furthermore, the Chair is sensitive to the fact that hon. members may wish to retain for themselves the prerogative of resubmitting notices, because in framing each successive application they have the opportunity to capture with precision the changing elements which give rise to the request for an emergency debate and which may bear heavily on the ultimate success of the application.

The Budget
I would ask hon. members to remember that on a number of occasions when applications have come to the Chair and I have decided not to proceed with an adjournment of House business for an emergency debate, I have often remarked that it would not be appropriate to do so, and I use the words "at this time". The reason for that, of course, is that circumstances can change very rapidly, especially in an area where there is concern with respect to the necessity to have an emergency debate.

The Chair is pleased to have had this opportunity to relate to the House the considerations which have informed its decision to continue the existing practice with regard to notices submitted pursuant to Standing Order 52.

I thank hon. members for their assistance in this matter.

I also heard some comments, not always veiy favourable, on the Budget brought down on February 20 by the Minister of Finance Although not everyone was satisfied with the Budget, all the people I talked to saw the Budget and the minister's agenda as an expression of the government's will to provide even more efficient management and to bring the deficit and our national debt under control.

The Budget
Madam Speaker, this is the Progressive Conservative Government's sixth Budget, and once again, it reflects the government's thoroughly consistent and serious approach to meeting its objectives. It is the culmination of five years of hard work during which the government has reviewed and updated regulatory procedures, revamped our tax system by lowering tax rates and eliminating loopholes, abolished trade barriers, improved manpower training programs and turned around the country's economic situation.
Despite gloomy forecasts, over 1.5 million jobs were created since the beginning of our term, and among the major industrial countries, only Japan's economic performance outshipped ours. However, to provide for an even more prosperous future, we must eliminate our deficit and reduce the debt, making Canadians less vulnerable to the impact of interest rates and to inflation which is a threat to us all. They will feel more secure and will be able to operate even more effectively.
We must act now, in a manner that is both effective and compassionate, to control our debt while maintaining the programs and services we cherish. This is the only way we can preserve a climate conducive to maintaining our economic, social and psychological development.

Previous Liberal governments encouraged Canadians to depend on government and often forced them to do so. After the war, the central government was given a mandate to help the country and its citizens recover from a situation that had destabilized the economy. We had to reconvert from a wartime to a peacetime economy. This position was sound because we had a vigorous economic recovery. The reconversion went well. However, instead of letting Canadians continue to become more dynamic, the government decided to keep on exercising power by controlling the economic levers rather than trusting Canadians. It wanted to keep the leading role and increase the process of centralization, thereby keeping the spotlight on its supposedly brilliant performance.
Under Mr. Trudeau, who claimed to have contempt for nationalists, the government and he showed a distrustful nationalism towards the Americans and the obvious differences among the provinces. This mistrust resulted in undue control and supervision, as with the Foreign Investment Review Agency; the nationalization of several industries could only lead to increased dependence.
He succeeded in developing passive behaviour and discouraging, if not killing, creativity and innovation. Everywhere people showed "sweet indifference".
We reached the point, Madam Speaker, where someone who was thinking of starting a new project would first find out what grant programs were available. By repeating that people had rights, we made them forget that they also had duties and resources. We were depriving them of the pride that comes from doing something oneself. We were preparing poorly for future challenges.
We all know that in a competitive world like today's, only the most inventive and most able to benefit from their environment can win.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to deliver a statement on the Commonwealth on this special day of honouring it as an international organization.
The Commonwealth is a very unusual international organization. Once an empire, it has become an institution comprised of nearly one-quarter of the world's population. Almost every race, religious faith, culture and level of economic development can be found in the Commonwealth fold. Composed of 50 independent states, its members range from aligned to non-aligned and have all shades of ideological opinion.
The Commonwealth is an essentially multinational body of equal sovereign members with a common concern for international peace and a commitment to the economic development of member countries. Consultation and co-operation govern this association.
The Commonwealth's ties are informal and diverse. It possesses none of the attributes generally attached to an international political association. There is no constitution. The association does not encroach on the sovereignty of individual members, it has no common foreign policy and does not require its members to reach collective decisions or to take united action. There is nothing formally or legally binding the member states together.
Yet the Commonwealth is a very compatible organization. This can be traced to the fact that all member states were former British colonies in one way or another. Members share the basic traditions of respect for the

Routine Proceedings
British parliamentary democracy, the rule of law and the rights of individuals and minorities.
The Commonwealth has been doing for years what similar organizations are just starting to accept and to implement. Members do not strive to solve political problems, but work towards reducing strains and easing tensions in order to provide a framework in which differences can begin to be reconciled. The Commonwealth if definitely given to practicality. It can deal as effectively with the great problems of the day as it can with everyday problems.
The heads of government in the Commonwealth meet on a regular basis. These meetings are often the testing grounds for ideas. The results of such meetings are often noteworthy. For instance, the Declaration of Commonwealth Principles and the establishment of a fund for technical co-operation in 1971, the Lusaka declaration of 1979 opposing racism and racial prejudice, and the Melbourne declaration of 1981 expressing a determination to end global poverty and inequality.
Countries small and large have a voice within the Commonwealth. Twenty-six member states have populations that number less than one million. The Commonwealth is often the most significant link these countries have with the rest of the world. The Commonwealth is, as a result, the best advocate for the special needs and problems of these small countries. As virtually every region of the world is represented in the Commonwealth, it is easy to see that membership helps more than it hinders.
"India has contacts with southeast Asian states which no other Commonwealth country can match. Canada has an unrivalled knowledge of the United States; Britain has knowledge of Europe. Jamaica has a special advantage in understanding the countries of the Caribbean" and so can advises others. This becomes important as we move towards increasing global trade.
Both Canada and the Commonwealth have benefited from our membership. Not only have we helped to preserve the association in times of crisis and supported
all its programs, but we have been led to change some of our attitudes, especially those towards the Third World.
I recall attending a Caribbean Commonwealth Conference in 1973 as an observer with two former MPs, Senator Heath Macquarrie and the present Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, Lincoln Alexander. At the beginning of the conference, the chairman stood up and said: "We want our three Canadian friends who are here as observers to feel free to intervene in our proceedings any time they wish to speak, for Canada is the best friend the Caribbean Commonwealth countries have in the world. On that trip, I flew to a cadet training camp to visit with 30 Canadian cadets who were there to train for a month with other cadets from Commonwealth countries. A memorandum of understanding is meant to serve two purposes. Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, during the course of discussions it was agreed that the crop insurance legislation had to be renewed and improved to provide for a more equitable sharing of federal-provincial costs and to enhance the program to reflect the realities of today and the current decade.
This legislation will reform the act to provide producers with guaranteed protection against losses caused by natural disasters. It will also ensure the best insurance coverage available at an affordable cost to the largest number of producers.



March 19, 1990

One of the major areas of change modifies the calculations which were used to determine the level of protection producers will be eligible to insure. The current act provides a method of predicting yield based on the simple historical average of a producer or of a geographic area. This method has been considered by producers to be inflexible and even punitive.
Bill C-48 provides new approaches to determine insurable yields and these approaches will take into account the use of new technology by producers. It will also buffer producers' yield calculation for successive losses, particularly in western Canada. We have had a situation where the historical average fell because of successive years of drought and other weather related disasters. I might say that the last three or four years in western Canada, in terms of the levels of precipitation and heat have probably been more severe than that experienced during the Dirty Thirties. So you have a problem of successive droughts where the over-all average is reduced triggering the lower level and thereby the producer does not get what would usually be considered a reflection of his normal crop.
Bill C-48 provides new approaches to determine insurable yield. As I said, the government will take into account, not only the new technology and methods of production, but also this problem of successive losses.
The amendments also allow the provinces to offer qualifying producers the option of insuring low risk crops at a higher level of protection. For example, the farmer could qualify to insure a crop at 90 percentage coverage instead of the current 80 per cent.
The provinces will now also have the flexibility of basing unit prices on market value or on cost of production. Again, this incorporates a very important item that will enhance the over-all operations of the crop insurance program.
Another major change being proposed under Bill C-48 provides for more equitable cost sharing arrangements that recognize agriculture is a shared responsibility between the federal and provincial governments.
Government Orders
Under the current act, the most commonly used formula allows provinces to pay all the administrative costs, while the federal government and the producers pick up the share of the premium on a fifty-fifty basis.
Under these amendments the federal and provincial governments will share all administrative costs and 50 per cent of the premiums. Producers will remain at the same proportion, namely paying 50 per cent of the premium and nothing towards the cost of administration.
This is an approach that most provinces favour in the over-all amending approach, the over-all improvements that we see incorporated in this legislation.
This approach will make the cost to governments more equitable, while at the same time provide for additional federal funding for improved program administration, including more producer education about the program.
I should say here that while the percentage of federal government spending, particularly as it relates to the premium, will be reduced. The federal government's over-all financial support of the program is expected to rise above traditional levels because of the enhancements. That was clearly the trade-off in working through the improvements to the crop insurance program.
Enhancements to the program, combined with increased participation and contributions to administration costs will increase federal expenditures under this program above historical levels.
Another proposed change will strengthen the crop insurance regulations. Regulatory provisions are being rewritten to set out clearly the basis for federal contributions to crop insurance. We got into a bit of that debate the other day where the hon. members were suggesting that because we use the words "up to 25 per cent", there was some concern that that would not be the case. That clearly is the case and it is now accidentally or otherwise enshrined in the legislation.
Special provisions are also contained in the new bill that recognize the importance of diversifying agriculture production. engage in new crop production and new plant production. This will provide more flexibility again in ensuring that adequate coverage will be available to cover new crops and that they will not be penalized.
The final major change is a special provision to compensate producers when their crops are damaged by migratory waterfowl. This provision recognizes the federal government's responsibility under international treaty to protect migratory waterfowl. The amendments propose to increase the compensation to 80 per cent of the actual value of the crops damaged.
I have been informed as well of the views expressed by the members of the legislative committee on additional ways to improve the program. I will take them into account before proposing regulations to the Governor in Council and in developing federal provincial agreements with each province. The provinces, as the insurers, have to know precisely what the terms and conditions governing the federal contribution are going to be as of April 1, 1990.

One way to accomplish this is to reduce the service the federal government has provided in the past. The cost of a program is passed on to the provincial government, the municipality, the farmer, or the consumer. Another way to reduce cost is to pass the service on to some other organization which then proceeds to charge a fee to provide that service and make it an extra cost to the farmer.

Madam Speaker, as hon. members are aware-

The Financial Administration Act requires that statutory borrowing authority be obtained from Parliament in order for the government to increase its outstanding debt.
Specifically, Part IV, section 36 of the act requires that "no money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of Parliament". This refers to new money only rather than the refinancing of existing debt since section 46 of the act provides continuing authority to borrow funds to repay maturing debt.
While section 47 provides for temporary short-term borrowings, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament to permit the government to implement a regular debt program to meet its financial requirements.
This bill should be viewed in the context of the government's continuing efforts to deal with Canada's deficit and debt problem.
The budget tabled by the Minister of Finance on February 20 reaffirms the government's commitment to reduce the deficit. Through a wide-ranging expenditure control plan and with no increase in taxes, the budget keeps the deficit on a downward path that will see it cut in half in four years.
The budget is part of the government's consistent, comprehensive plan to ensure that Canadians benefit from a strong and prosperous Canada.
That plan, first set out in 1984, has two main thrusts: to foster a dynamic, innovative and competitive private sector; and to put the government's fiscal house in order.
Our economic plan and the firm actions we have taken in the budget as part of that plan have brought us a clear prospect of lower inflation and a steadily declining deficit. They help ensure that the government's fiscal position in the 1990s can support the programs Canadians value most. By persevering, we will attain great control over our destiny and greater ability to devote our resources to investments in a rising standard of living and a better quality of life for all Canadians.
I would now like to outline for the House the terms of the borrowing authority bill for 1990-91. Paragraph 2(1) of the bill requests borrowing authority in the amount of $25.5 billion for fiscal 1990-91. This amount is equal to $22.5 billion of borrowing requirements, of which $21 billion is the government's estimated net financial requirements from the budget, $1.5 billion is the estimated exchange fund account earnings, and a $3 billion reserve to manage foreign exchange transactions.
As was the case last year, the request for borrowing authority to cover exchange fund earnings reflects the fact that although these earnings are reported in the public accounts as budgetary revenues, they give rise to additional Canadian dollarborrowing requirements. This is because they are retained in the exchange fund account and are not available to finance ongoing operations of the government.
The $3 billion reserve requested in the borrowing bill is the same as granted in the previous three years.
Paragraph 2(2) states that all unused borrowing authority granted by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1990-91, to the extent that the unused authority exceeds $3 billion, will be cancelled on March 31, 1991. Thus, this
March 22, 1990

paragraph preserves the government's non-lapsing reserve into the next year to accommodate the possibility that new statutory borrowing authority is not provided before the 1991-92 fiscal year begins.
Paragraph 3 ensures that the $3 billion reserve granted last fiscal year by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1989-90 will be cancelled on March 31, 1990 or on the date the new bill comes into force, whichever is later. Thus, this paragraph prevents non-lapsing reserves granted for earlier years from accumulating but ensures that cancellation will take place at a time that is not disruptive.
Paragraph 4 ensures that if the new bill passes after March 31, 1990 and part of the $3 billion reserve granted for 1989-90 has been used, this does not increase the total amount of borrowing authority available for 1990-91.
For the information of hon. members, I would like to briefly review the government's debt operations to the end of February 1989-90.
So far the domestic debt program has increased the unmatured domestic debt outstanding by approximately $19.6 billion. At the same time the outstanding debt in foreign currencies has been reduced by $2.9 billion. The combined effect has been an increase in the outstanding unmatured debt to around $294 billion.
Of the total net debt issued so far in 1989-1990, $10 billion was in the form of marketable bonds. As well, the government increased the emphasis on selling bonds by auction, which it has found to be a cost effective form of issuing debt. Auctions now account for about 65 per cent of all marketable bonds issued, up from about 60 per cent in 1988-89.
Treasury bills were used to raise $15.5 billion of new funds to the end of February 1989-90.
This fall the 1989 Canada Savings Bond campaign with a coupon of 10.5 per cent generated total sales of $9.3 billion. The net amount raised in the campaign, after taking account of CSBs which matured in 1989 and other maturities which were redeemed during the campaign, was $3.1 billion.
In closing, I would like to remind hon. members that they have all the necessary information before them to deal with this bill. The bill is related to the borrowing
Government Orders
requirements set out in the budget and the Estimates which have been tabled in the House.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, and I hope that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken) and other members of the opposition will help expedite the passage of this bill through the House.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I also thank my colleagues.
The 1987 program also included coverage for summer fallow acreage in western Canada.
The federal government also came to the aid of farmers with the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program. This program was developed in response to the drought of 1988 which caused heavy crop damage in many regions of Canada.
In western Canada the 1988 crop totalled just over 31 million tonnes in comparison to a slightly below average 40.7 million in 1989. Farmers who suffered the most severe drought losses in 1988 were assisted through the $850 million federal drought program, which was applicable to all parts of Canada.
In addition, the federal government improved crop insurance programs to strengthen protection for farmers from similar catastrophes. In 1989, as a result of the

severe drought losses of the previous year, the federal government reviewed the crop insurance program. As a result the program is more responsive and coverage is more extensive.
For example, before the changes to crop insurance in 1989 the payment for wheat on stubble in Saskatchewan would have ranged between $32.23 and $52.91 per acre, depending on the risk area. In 1989 the payment for wheat on stubble in the same risk area would range from $49.81 to $85.17 per acre. That is considerably higher coverage.
These changes to crop insurance demonstrate how the federal government is responding to the need for farm income stability. A bill is currently before the House which will result in further improvements to the crop insurance program. The special assistance programs I have mentioned helped farmers with assistance when it was most needed.
But as we know, providing ad hoc assistance is not the most desirable away to produce a sensitive, responsive safety net for Canadian grain and oilseed farmers. Farmers from all regions agree that they need a comprehensive regional safety net program which is fair to all grain and oilseed producers.
Efforts to achieve that are under way. As part of the federal government's agricultural policy review, a special committee of industry and government is working now to develop proposals for a new national grain safety net program.
The Grains Safety Net Committee was formed following a national agri-food conference in Ottawa last December. At that conference it was agreed that we had to move urgently on the development of a better safety net for grain farmers. Our Minister of Agriculture gave this issue a high priority and put it on the fast track.
This committee is looking at a number of different safety net options for grain and oilseed farmers. It is expected the committee will be ready to present its proposals to federal and provincial agriculture ministers in late spring.
The Grains Safety Net Committee is just one of many similar groups now working on agricultural issues as part of a comprehensive agricultural policy review.
Private Members' Business
Defining the problems facing farmers was the first step in this review. Now the job at hand is to develop options, consult with the industry on these options and, finally, take decisions. This applies in all areas under review: marketing, trade development and value added, financial management, safety nets, supply management, transportation, food safety and quality, and sustainable agriculture.
Grain and oilseed farmers are among those most in need of income stabilization at this time. The federal government is responding to that need, as it has done in the past.
The federal government is clearly committed to ensuring, to the greatest extent possible, that our grain and oilseed industry remains viable and productive. Our producers have not and will not be left at the mercy of international trading practices or extraordinary weather conditions over which they have no control. The government's record is proof of its concern.
The policy review is added proof. This wide-ranging review is designed to address concerns with a view to building a healthy, prosperous future for the Canadian agri-food industry. It is the most comprehensive review of Canadian agriculture ever undertaken.
At this time it makes sense to look at the issues such as stabilization for farm-fed grain in the context of the over-all policy review. Now is not the time for piecemeal changes. Now is the time for dealing with issues in a comprehensive way. It is a way that will bring lasting benefits to all Canadian farmers.

The motion only asks the government to consider doing something about the effect of paying stabilization on grain that is sold commercially but not paying stabilization on farm-fed grain.
I have to commend my colleague for bringing in a motion like this one because it is time well spent.
When you stop and look at the rationale behind the motion, you have to realize that those producers who grow their own grain are always in the same cycle. When the prices of grain are low, the livestock prices are low as well.

March 22, 1990
Private Members' Business
I hope hon. members opposite vote in the true spirit of this motion and not oppose it simply because it comes from this side of the House.
I can tell you from past experience that the way the stabilization act works now is not fair. A farmer who produces his own grain for consumption by his own herd of cattle or hogs cannot be part of the program since he has to subtract what he purchased from what he sold. There is no net benefit.
However, if a fanner is the sole producer of grain, he can be involved in the stabilization program. If he is the purchaser of feeds, he cannot benefit from that.
I believe that a sale should be a sale, no matter which way it goes. As my colleague from Prince Edward-Hastings mentioned last month, whether he sells as a primary producer, whether he sells to the local grain elevator his own grain enterprise in a farming operation, a hog enterprise or a beef producing enterprise, a sale should be a sale.
The current Western Grain Stabilization Act is not fair. The agricultural industry has been waiting and asking for changes to this legislation for a long time.
I remind the House that the following organizations support this kind of move: the three prairie wheat pools, turkey producers, the Sheep Marketing Agency, the Pork Producers Marketing Board, the Milk Marketing Board, the Egg Producers Marketing Board, the chicken producers, the Canadian Pork Council, the Ontario Cattlemen's Association, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and the UPA of Quebec which is probably the largest farm organization in Canada, as well as many other groups and individuals.
Fanners who chose to use all the grain on their farm were in effect told by the signals of the stabilization act that their type of production was no longer needed and was not appreciated. The end result was that they received less money for their grain production than their neighbour down the road. It sounds like the drought assistance program, and we all know what happened with the drought assistance program.
The mandate that the government gave the review committee referred to boundaries. The Lord knows no boundaries. Mother nature knows no boundaries.
A lot of people in my riding averaged seven bushels of beans to the acre and 48 bushels of com to the acre when the five-year average for beans was 50 bushels and for com 142 bushels. These people received nothing. This year for their start-up they have no funding. The program was a disaster.
The administration of the proposal in the motion will not be as difficult as members opposite will say. It has been tried in Alberta, and it is now being copied in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The formula is there.
It could be applied under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, to provide a payment for farm-fed grains.
There would no longer be discrimination against those producers who chose to feed dairy cattle, poultry or livestock on the farm.
In this House we must all be vigilant to protect our agricultural industry. It is certainly important in my riding and we wonder about the government's priorities. Madam Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to speak today in support of this motion from my colleague. At the outset I would like to focus my comments on the preamble of his motion because March 21 was the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of Agnes MacPhail, the first woman

elected to this House and an untiring champion of the rights of rural Canadians.
To begin my remarks I would like to quote from Hansard of February 28, 1928. Although that was 1928, it says a lot about what is occurring here now in 1990. During the debate on the budget of that year Agnes MacPhail stated:
We have, for a young and rich country, a depleted and impoverished agricultural industry. In this young country agriculture has not held its own people, nor its power of place and influence. I regret it, but it is true.
It is still true. Many of the things that Agnes MacPhail struggled for in her years in Parliament we are still struggling for now. Agnes MacPhail was in this place for almost 20 years from 1921 to 1940 and then continued in the Ontario legislature.
To win her first nomination in 1921, she had to defeat 10 men and then overcome the shock in the community that a woman had won. She then won the first of five federal elections with a campaign that cost $600, all in $1 contributions. There were no special favours from Agnes. At 31 she entered a House that was hardly ready for her. She was patronized by the Mackenzie King government which offered her a suite of offices when other MPs had only one room. Agnes took one room. It was then room 605 which became Agnes' office for her career, and it is now redesignated as room 629-C. This week my leader unveiled a plaque to be placed on the door of that room to commemorate Agnes' time there.
Agnes also met outright hostility in this House but learned to deal with it. To the heckler who taunted: "Doesn't the hon. member wish she were a man?" she replied: "No. Doesn't the hon. member wish he were?"
These quotes are very in keeping with some of the debate that goes on in this Chamber even now, Madam Speaker, and as you are well aware, women do have an uphill struggle even now in this Chamber.
My remarks on this motion speak to the legacy that Agnes MacPhail has left for us as women to carry on. In the most recent budget, there have been radical cuts to women's programs. I was the volunteer chair of a women's centre in my community when the parliamentary committee travelled to Vancouver to talk about women's programs a number of years ago.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the borrowing authority is traditionally an occasion in the House of Commons when members are able to debate economic policy of the government, and it is my regret that on this occasion the government has chosen to cut off debate before that discussion has taken place. There is certainly much to be said about the government's failure to provide real economic leadership in our economy, real economic leadership to the Canadian people.

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
It is a well known tenet of basic economics that a short-term deficit can be a major way of promoting growth and demand during a downturn in a business cycle. The opposite side of that equation is that when the economy re-enters a period of growth, public expenditure must be reined in, both to reduce inflationaiy pressures in the economy and to repay the debt which the government incurred when it was stimulating the economy.
This government has shown no evidence of real commitment to constraint in its spending during the past eight years of remarkable prosperity; prosperity I might point out which was to a substantial degree triggered and augmented by the spending of the previous government during a period of economic recession.
The single failure of this government to employ both fiscal and monetary policy to restore our economy to growth and expansion is everywhere evident. Since the 1981 recession, Canada has experienced uninterrupted economic growth. Yet during this period the government has allowed the public debt to more than double. The public debt is well over twice today what it was when this government entered office.
In 1988, for example, the net financial debt of the federal government, the provincial governments and the local governments across Canada was about $400 billion or over $15,000 for every Canadian. Among the other major members of the OECD, only Britain and Italy had a higher debt to gross national product ratio.
The growth of this debt is of even more concern than its size. Admittedly, there has been some modest progress in reducing the ratio of expenditures to revenue. In 1984, when the deficit reached its peak, federal expenditures were equal to 24 per cent of GDP, whereas federal revenues were only 17 per cent. By 1988, the government reminds us, federal expenditures had dropped to 21 per cent of GDP and revenues through tax increases had risen to over 18 per cent. These modest gains were more than offset by the dramatic rise in interest rates and accordingly in debt service charges.
According to the finance minister's last budget, average interest rates for the next year are forecast at over 11 per cent, while Canada's growth rate will average no more than 2 per cent.
When interest rates are higher than the rate of growth, the stage obviously is set for a further explosion in the public debt. Under these circumstances, the primary budget, that is excluding net interest payments, must generate a surplus sufficient to offset the growth in interest costs, if an increase in the debt is to be avoided. In other words, increases in revenue and reductions in government expenditure are both needed simply to overcome the rising costs of the public debt. Yet there is no evidence that interest rates will fall dramatically in the short-term, despite the Finance Minister's optimistic predictions.
Largely as a result of six years of government overspending, inflation is now running at more than 5 per cent. Moreover, escalating rates in Japan and in western Europe will force the Bank of Canada, if it chooses to continue its present policies, to raise its own interest rates if Canada wants to continue to attract foreign capital and to maintain international confidence in our dollar.
This afternoon, I think we will see interest rates increase yet again. There is certainly every reason to believe that interest rates will be even higher than those forecast by the Minister of Finance not a month ago.
What are the implications for Canadians of this mismanagement of our economy? First, we increase our net foreign liabilities. Of course, many Canadian corporations, public utilities and provincial governments traditionally have borrowed abroad. Recently, however, the national government also has turned to offshore borrowing as a way of financing its debt and its expenditures. About 30 per cent of Canadian Government bonds are now held by foreigners. With the current high levels of interest, an increasing share of wealth will now be siphoned off abroad in order to pay those debts.
Moreover, the Canadian government will become that much more addicted to high interest rates and a high Canadian dollar, if it is to continue to attract the high levels of foreign capital it believes that it needs to finance its operations and its growing debt.
March 29, 1990

The second major implication for Canada is that private investment will be discouraged by the present fiscal and monetary policies of this government. The high levels of taxation needed to finance the federal deficit has undoubtedly served to crowd out domestic investment. The Canadian economy today needs about $100 billion a year to finance itself. But since only $40 billion of this can be supplied from consumer savings in Canada, the economy looks offshore for almost $60 billion a year.
Moreover, the government's failure to solve its debt problem has raised further concerns about future levels of taxation. That, in turn, undoubtedly discourages private sector capital formation.
Further, given the current differential between domestic and international interest rates, Canadian businesses are encouraged to draw upon foreign savings, and these foreign borrowings have in turn pushed exchange rates for the Canadian dollar far beyond what our productivity would seem to warrant. The implications of a high Canadian dollar for our existing and future trade opportunities, particularly in light of our increased vulnerability to the United States, is obvious.

Mr. Speaker, on March 26, 1990, I rose in this House to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to intervene to help Leonid and Natalia Stonov. They have been waiting for almost 12 years to get their exit visas to leave the U.S.S.R. and go to Israel.
They first applied to leave in 1979, almost 12 years ago. They last applied in 1988. At that time were not only turned down again but were told: "Do not apply for at least another four years".
The reason for the latest refusal in 1988 was that Leonid possesses state secrets. Mr. Stonov was a herbol-ogist. He has not practised his profession in over 10 years. How could he possibly possess, at this stage, state secrets that would worry the U.S.S.R.?
Even Mr. Gorbachev has stated that, in most cases, the state secrecy rule should not apply beyond five years. How could the Stonov's case possibly be an exception to that statement by Mr. Gorbachev?
On Sunday, March 25,1990,1 met with Natalia Stonov at Beth Tikvah Synagogue in Willowdale. She was in Canada on a visitor's visa. The Stonovs have been adopted by the Congregation of Beth Tikvah Synagogue.
On that morning we contacted Leonid Stonov in Moscow. It was thrilling to talk to him.
Leonid is one of the leading members of the Refusnik community in Moscow. Perhaps that is why he has been treated so cruelly for over 10 years.
He and Natalia, who is a physician, have both been stripped of their academic degrees and were once arrested for parasitic behaviour. In other words, they were unemployed.

April 3, 1990
Adjournment Debate
While I want to condemn the Soviet authorities for their treatment of individuals such as the Stonovs, there are hundreds of Refusniks like them.
It is time that the Soviet Union totally lived up to its human rights obligations. How can it possibly be planning to host an international conference on human rights next year, 1991, in Moscow when these cruel abuses continue?
There is an urgent need to deal humanely and compassionately with these long-term Refusniks. On the other hand, I compliment Mr. Gorbachev for his introduction of glasnost which means more openness and perestroika which means restructuring.
From a human rights standpoint, and to be fair, the record must show that an incredible number of Jews have received exit visas in recent years.
Let the record show that in 1986, when I was elected chairman of the Canadian Parliamentary Group for Soviet Jewry, only 914 Jews obtained exit visas.
I led a small all-party delegation to the U.S.S.R. in 1987. We met with more than 150 Refusniks and with several Soviet officials. There were some positive signals but the climate was rigid and uncompromising. Glasnost had been announced and Mr. Gorbachev was obviously insisting that changes must be made. In 1987, more than 8,000 Jews received exit visas. In 1988, the number climbed to more than 18,000, and last year, 1989, more than 70,000 Jews obtained their exit visas.
While glasnost has brought some progress on human rights, it has also revealed a dark side. With more openness in letters to the editors in newspapers, on TV and in books, many people are fanning the flames of anti-Semitic behaviour. This is a most regrettable and despicable development. Because of the vile nature of these anti-Semitic fanatics, many thousands more Jews now want to leave the U.S.S.R. Jews have become the scapegoats of perestroika.
However, increasingly the way to the Jewish state is blocked. After 23 years of a diplomatic stalemate, no direct flights between Israel and the Soviet Union exist. The only way for Soviet Jews to reach Israel is to disembark at some airport in Europe and then arrange a direct flight to Tel Aviv. Hungarian Airlines recently cancelled its Moscow-Budapest-Tel Aviv flights due to threats from Arab terrorists.
Last week, over 200 members of the U.S. Congress signed a letter to His Excellency Yuriy Dubinin, ambassador of the Soviet Union in Washington. In the letter, they said that they were appalled and dismayed to learn that the Government of the Soviet Union had rejected an appeal from President George Bush and Secretary Baker to permit direct flights for Soviet Jews from Moscow to Israel.
I call upon the Canadian government to work with other democratic governments in the east and the west to help arrange for direct flights from the U.S.S.R. to Israel. The backlog of Soviet Jews with exit visas waiting to leave the U.S.S.R. is in the tens of thousands. This is a human rights time bomb.
In summary, there are three issues that we as Canadian parliamentarians must solve. We cannot solve these issues ourselves. We need the support of other democratic countries.
First, we must continue to pressure the Soviet authorities to deal quickly and compassionately with individual Refusnik cases such as the Stonovs. Let us not have the large volume of Jews receiving their exit visas overshadow the cruel plight of individual Refusniks such as the Stonovs.
Secondly, a way must be found to arrange for direct flights from the U.S.S.R. to Israel.
Third, leaders of the western world must speak up about the ugly consequences of unbridled anti-Semitism.
These are awesome challenges, but this should not deter men and women of good faith to tackle these challenges with all their energy and resources.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has indicated, the decision with respect to the Oldman came down about three weeks ago. That decision, of course, was contrary to an earlier decision of the Federal Court.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, as most hon. members know, the province of Alberta has given indication of its intent to apply for leave to the Supreme Court to appeal. In the meantime, departmental officials in conjunction with other related departments, as I have already said, have been very closely investigating not only how we should respond to the Oldman, which I think is an appropriate deliberation on our part, but how we should also respond to each and every other project which has been proposed within the country that might have implications for the federal government.
We are doing that and those decisions will be announced in due course.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.
